Stationary Bias and Extrapolation in Nonlinear Two-Timescale Stochastic Approximation

A.Ch. Madhusudanarao Affiliation: Department of Computer Science and Automation Affiliation: Indian Institute of Science, Bengaluru, India Email: madhusudanar@iisc.ac.in    Rahul Singh Affiliation: Laboratoire de Recherche de l’EPITA, Paris, France Email: rahulsingh0188@gmail.com
Abstract

Constant-step stochastic approximation generally has a nonzero stationary mean error that persists under time averaging. This paper studies that error for nonlinear two-timescale recursions driven by an exogenous finite-state Markov chain. Under stated smoothness assumptions and conditions on the stationary distribution, we derive a first-order bias expansion whose error bound remains uniform as the slow step size becomes much smaller than the fast step size. Fast-manifold coordinates keep the associated covariance equation regular in this limit. For fast step η\eta and slow step ε\varepsilon, the expansion reveals a mixed contribution ε2/η\varepsilon^{2}/\eta alongside terms linear in each step size. This dependence matters for bias reduction: along power-law step-size paths, the bias exponents need not be integers, so Richardson–Romberg extrapolation requires weights matched to the path. An exactly solvable nonlinear Markov example verifies the coefficients. We verify localization for temporal-difference learning and compare finite-run extrapolation at equal update budgets. For finite runs, we bound the initialization error of tail averages on both timescales under an additional coupling assumption. In the special case of additive independent noise, signed third-moment cancellation yields a sharper remainder.

1 Introduction

Stochastic approximation (SA) studies iterative algorithms that update their variables using noisy observations. Constant-step SA generally approaches an invariant distribution whose mean differs from the equilibrium of the averaged dynamics. This difference is the stationary bias. Averaging the iterates zkz_{k} to give z¯N=N−1​∑k=1Nzk\bar{z}_{N}=N^{-1}\sum_{k=1}^{N}z_{k} reduces fluctuations but retains this stationary bias since under stationarity 𝔼​z¯N=𝔼​z1\mathbb{E}\bar{z}_{N}=\mathbb{E}z_{1}.

In two-timescale SA, two coupled sets of variables are updated with different step sizes. Write the fast step as η\eta, the slow step as ε\varepsilon, and their ratio as ρ=ε/η\rho=\varepsilon/\eta. Our goal is to determine how these two rates jointly affect the stationary bias. The connection to covariance comes from nonlinearity: a Taylor expansion of the averaged update around equilibrium contains quadratic terms whose expectations involve products of coordinate fluctuations. Consequently, the leading curvature contribution to the mean bias depends on the stationary covariance. Correlations between the current iterate and the observation can produce an additional bias contribution, which our analysis also accounts for.

To determine this covariance, we expand the stationary balance of second moments near equilibrium. At leading order, contraction under the linearized dynamics balances the fluctuations supplied by the noise. This balance takes the form of a Lyapunov equation, a linear matrix equation for the leading covariance coefficient. For temporally correlated observations, its noise covariance includes correlations across time. Solving and controlling this equation is therefore an intermediate step in computing the nonlinear mean bias.

The difficulty is obtaining covariance estimates that remain useful as ρ↓0\rho\downarrow 0. On the fast clock, where kk iterations correspond to time t=k​ηt=k\eta, the slow drift is scaled by ρ\rho. A scalar slow mode v˙=−a​ρ​v\dot{v}=-a\rho v, a>0a>0, for example, decays as e−a​ρ​te^{-a\rho t}. Thus the slow spectral gap, the smallest exponential decay rate among the slow linearized modes, tends to zero with ρ\rho. Bounds for the Lyapunov equation accumulate perturbations over this decay time and can introduce a factor 1/ρ1/\rho, as illustrated by ∫0∞e−2​a​ρ​t​𝑑t=(2​a​ρ)−1\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-2a\rho t}\,dt=(2a\rho)^{-1}. However, the noise and remainder terms in the slow covariance equation also carry small powers of ρ\rho. Retaining these factors prevents an artificial loss of uniformity and allows the covariance estimate to support a uniform bias expansion.

We study nonlinear recursions driven by an exogenous finite-state Markov chain: the next input depends on the input history only through its current state, and its transition law is unaffected by the algorithm. We obtain a first-order stationary bias expansion uniform in small positive ρ\rho, meaning that the remainder constant does not diverge as ρ↓0\rho\downarrow 0. Coordinates relative to the fast equilibrium manifold, the local family of equilibria of the fast averaged dynamics as the slow variable varies, regularize the covariance equation by exposing the scales of its fast and slow blocks. Writing mη,ρm_{\eta,\rho} for the stationary mean displacement from equilibrium, we obtain

mη,ρ=η​b0+ε​b1+ε2η​b2+O⁡(η3/2+ε3η2).m_{\eta,\rho}=\eta b_{0}+\varepsilon b_{1}+\frac{\varepsilon^{2}}{\eta}b_{2}+O\!\left(\eta^{3/2}+\frac{\varepsilon^{3}}{\eta^{2}}\right).

Here b0,b1,b2b_{0},b_{1},b_{2} are coefficient vectors determined by the update rule and noise law, independent of the step sizes.

The mixed term matters for Richardson–Romberg extrapolation, which forms a weighted combination of estimates at different step sizes to cancel leading bias terms. Along the power-law path ε=ηp\varepsilon=\eta^{p}, p>1p>1, its exponent is 2​p−12p-1, alongside 11 and pp. We derive weights adapted to these powers and verify nonzero mixed bias in an exactly solvable nonlinear Markov model. We also bound the initialization error of tail averages, formed after discarding an initial segment of the trajectory, under an additional coupling assumption. This assumption controls the difference between a trajectory from a prescribed initial state and a stationary trajectory constructed on the same probability space. Stationary existence and localization, expressed through moment bounds around the equilibrium, are explicit hypotheses; local stability alone does not establish them.

We study fixed-policy value estimation using temporal-difference learning with gradient correction (TDC) [20]. We verify stationary localization through uniform block contraction and compare finite-run bias, variance, and mean-square error for ordinary averaging and extrapolation at equal update budgets.

Related work.

The ordinary differential equation (ODE) framework for SA is developed in [14, 3]. Decreasing-step two-timescale theory includes [2, 18]; finite-time results treat linear recursions [4], including Markov inputs [13] and nonlinear systems [6], with Markov central limit theory and applications to TDC and related gradient-TD methods in [10]. Invariant-distribution and weak-error analyses, which study errors in expectations of observables, appear for constant-step stochastic gradient methods in [5, 7]. Bias expansions and Richardson–Romberg correction for Markov SA are studied by Huo et al. [11], while Allmeier and Gast [1] compute first-order bias using Lyapunov equations. For nonlinear SA, Huo et al. [12] distinguish bias contributions from memory, nonlinearity, and their interaction. The closest two-timescale work, Kwon et al. [15], studies stationary laws, bias, variance, averaging, and extrapolation for linear recursions. Our work addresses nonlinear curvature and derives a covariance expansion uniform as the step-size ratio vanishes. Extrapolation methods are also developed in [8, 19, 17].

Notation.

Norms are Euclidean or induced matrix norms; ⊤\top denotes transpose. A matrix is Hurwitz if all its eigenvalues have negative real parts. Constants in uniform bounds are independent of 0<η≤η00<\eta\leq\eta_{0} and 0<ρ≤ρ00<\rho\leq\rho_{0}, with sufficiently small fixed upper bounds. Unless indicated otherwise, expectations are stationary.

2 Model and Assumptions

2.1 Recursion and Coordinates

Consider

xk+1\displaystyle x_{k+1} =xk+η​H​(Yk,xk,θk),\displaystyle=x_{k}+\eta H(Y_{k},x_{k},\theta_{k}), (1)
θk+1\displaystyle\theta_{k+1} =θk+ε​F​(Yk,xk,θk),\displaystyle=\theta_{k}+\varepsilon F(Y_{k},x_{k},\theta_{k}), (2)

where xk∈ℝdxx_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}}, θk∈ℝdθ\theta_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\theta}}, η>0\eta>0, and ε=η​ρ\varepsilon=\eta\rho with 0<ρ<10<\rho<1. Thus xkx_{k} uses the larger step size and θk\theta_{k} the smaller one. The uniform results below concern sufficiently small positive η\eta and ρ\rho.

The exogenous input (Yk)(Y_{k}) is a Markov chain on a finite state space 𝖸\mathsf{Y}, with transition matrix PP, i.e., ℙ⁡(Yk+1=y′∣ℱk)=P⁡(Yk,y′)\mathbb{P}(Y_{k+1}=y^{\prime}\mid\mathcal{F}_{k})=P(Y_{k},y^{\prime}), where ℱk\mathcal{F}_{k} is the sigma-field generated by the inputs and iterates through time kk. Its invariant distribution is μ\mu.

For a function aa on 𝖸\mathsf{Y}, write

P​a​(y)=∑y′P⁡(y,y′)​a​(y′),μ​a=∑yμ⁡(y)​a​(y).Pa(y)=\sum_{y^{\prime}}P(y,y^{\prime})a(y^{\prime}),\qquad\mu a=\sum_{y}\mu(y)a(y).

Set z=(x⊤,θ⊤)⊤z=(x^{\top},\theta^{\top})^{\top} and G⁡(y,z)=(H​(y,x,θ)⊤,F​(y,x,θ)⊤)⊤G(y,z)=(H(y,x,\theta)^{\top},F(y,x,\theta)^{\top})^{\top}. The averaged update field is

G¯​(z)=μ​G​(⋅,z)=(H¯​(x,θ)F¯​(x,θ)),\bar{G}(z)=\mu G(\cdot,z)=\binom{\bar{H}(x,\theta)}{\bar{F}(x,\theta)},

where the average is taken over the input while holding zz fixed. The joint recursion is therefore

Dρ=diag⁡(Idx,ρ​Idθ),zk+1=zk+η​Dρ​G​(Yk,zk).\begin{gathered}D_{\rho}=\operatorname{diag}(I_{d_{x}},\rho I_{d_{\theta}}),\\ z_{k+1}=z_{k}+\eta D_{\rho}G(Y_{k},z_{k}).\end{gathered} (3)

Fix an equilibrium z⋆=((x⋆)⊤,(θ⋆)⊤)⊤z^{\star}=((x^{\star})^{\top},(\theta^{\star})^{\top})^{\top} of the averaged field, so G¯​(z⋆)=0\bar{G}(z^{\star})=0. For each θ\theta near θ⋆\theta^{\star}, let λ⁡(θ)\lambda(\theta) denote the corresponding local equilibrium of the fast averaged dynamics:

H¯​(λ⁡(θ),θ)=0,λ⁡(θ⋆)=x⋆.\bar{H}(\lambda(\theta),\theta)=0,\qquad\lambda(\theta^{\star})=x^{\star}.

The local uniqueness and C2C^{2} regularity of this branch are specified in Assumption A1. The reduced slow drift is

g⁡(θ)=F¯​(λ⁡(θ),θ),g⁡(θ⋆)=0.g(\theta)=\bar{F}(\lambda(\theta),\theta),\qquad g(\theta^{\star})=0.

It describes the slow update when the fast variable is at the equilibrium associated with the current slow variable.

Define the Jacobian blocks, all evaluated at z⋆z^{\star}, by

A\displaystyle A =∂xH¯​(z⋆),\displaystyle=\partial_{x}\bar{H}(z^{\star}), B\displaystyle B =∂θH¯​(z⋆),\displaystyle=\partial_{\theta}\bar{H}(z^{\star}),
C\displaystyle C =∂xF¯​(z⋆),\displaystyle=\partial_{x}\bar{F}(z^{\star}), D\displaystyle D =∂θF¯​(z⋆).\displaystyle=\partial_{\theta}\bar{F}(z^{\star}).

The local stability assumption (Assumption A2) makes AA invertible. Differentiating the fast equilibrium identity H¯​(λ​(θ),θ)=0\bar{H}(\lambda(\theta),\theta)=0 gives A​D​λ​(θ⋆)+B=0AD\lambda(\theta^{\star})+B=0, and the chain rule then gives

J=D​G¯​(z⋆)=(ABCD),Λ=D​λ​(θ⋆)=−A−1​B,S=D​g​(θ⋆)=D+C​Λ=D−C​A−1​B.\begin{gathered}J=D\bar{G}(z^{\star})=\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\ C&D\end{pmatrix},\\ \Lambda=D\lambda(\theta^{\star})=-A^{-1}B,\\ S=Dg(\theta^{\star})=D+C\Lambda=D-CA^{-1}B.\end{gathered} (4)

Thus Λ\Lambda describes the first-order movement of the fast equilibrium as θ\theta changes, while SS is the Jacobian of the reduced slow drift.

To separate fast tracking from slow displacement, define locally

u^=x−λ⁡(θ),v=θ−θ⋆.\widehat{u}=x-\lambda(\theta),\qquad v=\theta-\theta^{\star}. (5)

Here u^\widehat{u} is the exact tracking error: it measures how far the fast variable is from the equilibrium associated with the current value of θ\theta. Replacing that equilibrium by its tangent approximation x⋆+Λ​vx^{\star}+\Lambda v gives the tangent tracking error u=x−x⋆−Λ​vu=x-x^{\star}-\Lambda v. Equivalently,

(uv)=T⁡(z−z⋆),T=(Idx−Λ0Idθ).\binom{u}{v}=T(z-z^{\star}),\qquad T=\begin{pmatrix}I_{d_{x}}&-\Lambda\\ 0&I_{d_{\theta}}\end{pmatrix}. (6)

‖rλ​(v)‖≤M2​‖v‖2(‖v‖≤r),\|r_{\lambda}(v)\|\leq\frac{M}{2}\|v\|^{2}\qquad(\|v\|\leq r),

The tangent coordinates also simplify the coupling in the equilibrium linearization. Using A​Λ+B=0A\Lambda+B=0, the linearized averaged recursion becomes

uk+1−uk\displaystyle u_{k+1}-u_{k} =η⁡[(A−ρ​Λ​C)​uk−ρ​Λ​S​vk],\displaystyle=\eta\bigl[(A-\rho\Lambda C)u_{k}-\rho\Lambda Sv_{k}\bigr],

2.2 Standing Assumptions

Write ek=zk−z⋆e_{k}=z_{k}-z^{\star} for the error process. For a stationary draw (Y,z)∼πη,ρ(Y,z)\sim\pi_{\eta,\rho} from a joint invariant law, define

e=z−z⋆,mη,ρ=𝔼​e,Γη,ρ=Cov⁡(e).e=z-z^{\star},\quad m_{\eta,\rho}=\mathbb{E}e,\quad\Gamma_{\eta,\rho}=\operatorname{Cov}(e). (7)

Thus ee is a stationary random vector, while mη,ρm_{\eta,\rho} and Γη,ρ\Gamma_{\eta,\rho} are its deterministic mean and covariance. All moments below are taken under πη,ρ\pi_{\eta,\rho}.

Assumption A1 (Local smoothness).

The averaged field G¯\bar{G} is C3C^{3} near z⋆z^{\star}. Near θ⋆\theta^{\star}, the fast equilibrium λ⁡(θ)\lambda(\theta) is locally unique and C2C^{2}, with λ⁡(θ⋆)=x⋆\lambda(\theta^{\star})=x^{\star}.

Assumption A2 (Local stability).

The matrices AA and SS in (4) are Hurwitz.

Assumption A3 (Mixing Markov input).

For some n0≥1n_{0}\geq 1, β>0\beta>0, and probability measure ν\nu on 𝖸\mathsf{Y}, Pn0​(y,E)≥β​ν​(E)P^{n_{0}}(y,E)\geq\beta\nu(E) for every y∈𝖸y\in\mathsf{Y} and every subset E⊆𝖸E\subseteq\mathsf{Y}.

Assumption A4 (Stationary fourth-moment localization).

There exist η0,ρ0,C>0\eta_{0},\rho_{0},C>0 such that, for every 0<η≤η00<\eta\leq\eta_{0} and 0<ρ≤ρ00<\rho\leq\rho_{0}, the joint process (Yk,zk)(Y_{k},z_{k}) admits an invariant law πη,ρ\pi_{\eta,\rho} satisfying

𝔼πη,ρ​‖z−z⋆‖4≤C​η2.\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\eta,\rho}}\|z-z^{\star}\|^{4}\leq C\eta^{2}. (8)

The constant CC is independent of η\eta and ρ\rho.

All stationary results refer to this selected family of invariant laws. Stationary existence and this moment bound do not follow from local Hurwitz stability alone. Proposition 4 gives sufficient conditions, and Appendix H.9 verifies localization for the nonlinear Markov example.

Assumption A5 (Update regularity).

Each G⁡(y,⋅)G(y,\cdot) is globally C2C^{2}, with

supy,z(‖Dz​G​(y,z)‖+‖Dz2​G​(y,z)‖)≤K.\sup_{y,z}\bigl(\|D_{z}G(y,z)\|+\|D_{z}^{2}G(y,z)\|\bigr)\leq K. (9)

These conditions allow updates growing linearly in zz. Together with local C3C^{3} smoothness and (8), they imply the expected Taylor estimates in Lemma 4. The stationary covariance and mean-bias expansions require no separate slow-coordinate moment or cross-covariance assumption. The stronger block and coordinate conditions in Assumption A7 are used only when invoking the supplementary blockwise fluctuation statements. The stationary iterates need not have bounded support.

3 Geometry, Noise, and Covariance

3.1 The Two Relaxation Clocks

On the fast timescale, where one iteration corresponds to time η\eta, the averaged ODE is z˙=Dρ​G¯​(z)\dot{z}=D_{\rho}\bar{G}(z). Its linearization at z⋆z^{\star}, expressed in the tangent coordinates w=T⁡(z−z⋆)w=T(z-z^{\star}), is w˙=Lρ​w\dot{w}=L_{\rho}w, where

Lρ=T​Dρ​J​T−1=(A−ρ​Λ​C−ρ​Λ​Sρ​Cρ​S).L_{\rho}=TD_{\rho}JT^{-1}=\begin{pmatrix}A-\rho\Lambda C&-\rho\Lambda S\\ \rho C&\rho S\end{pmatrix}. (10)

Thus et​Lρe^{tL_{\rho}} propagates an initial linearized perturbation over time tt; its subscripts below indicate the output and input coordinate groups. The following bounds separate the fast and slow decay rates and control their interaction, providing the linear estimates needed for uniform covariance analysis.

Proposition 1 (Two-clock semigroup bounds).

Under Assumptions A1–A2, there exist C∗,c,η0,ρ0>0C_{*},c,\eta_{0},\rho_{0}>0 such that for 0<ρ≤ρ00<\rho\leq\rho_{0} and t≥0t\geq 0,

‖[et​Lρ]u​u‖\displaystyle\|[e^{tL_{\rho}}]_{uu}\| ≤C∗​(e−c​t+ρ​e−c​ρ​t),\displaystyle\leq C_{*}(e^{-ct}+\rho e^{-c\rho t}), (11)
‖[et​Lρ]u​v‖+‖[et​Lρ]v​u‖\displaystyle\|[e^{tL_{\rho}}]_{uv}\|+\|[e^{tL_{\rho}}]_{vu}\| ≤C∗​ρ​(e−c​t+e−c​ρ​t),\displaystyle\leq C_{*}\rho(e^{-ct}+e^{-c\rho t}),
‖[et​Lρ]v​v‖\displaystyle\|[e^{tL_{\rho}}]_{vv}\| ≤C∗​e−c​ρ​t.\displaystyle\leq C_{*}e^{-c\rho t}.

For 0<η≤η00<\eta\leq\eta_{0} and integers k≥0k\geq 0, the same inequalities hold with et​Lρe^{tL_{\rho}} replaced by (I+η​Lρ)k(I+\eta L_{\rho})^{k}, and with e−c​te^{-ct} and e−c​ρ​te^{-c\rho t} replaced by e−c​η​ke^{-c\eta k} and e−c​ε​ke^{-c\varepsilon k}, respectively, where ε=η​ρ\varepsilon=\eta\rho.

Here (I+η​Lρ)k(I+\eta L_{\rho})^{k} propagates the linearized averaged recursion wk+1=(I+η​Lρ)​wkw_{k+1}=(I+\eta L_{\rho})w_{k} through kk iterations, corresponding to fast time t=η​kt=\eta k and slow time ρ​t=ε​k\rho t=\varepsilon k. The proof of both bounds is given in Appendix B.

3.2 Poisson Representation

We identify the effective covariance of the Markov noise, accounting for correlations across time. This supplies the noise term in the Lyapunov equation (14), whose solution determines the leading-order stationary covariance. The latter is used below to quantify how nonlinear drift converts fluctuations into stationary bias. To obtain the noise covariance, we use the Poisson equation introduced next.

For fixed zz, let G~​(y,z)=G⁡(y,z)−G¯​(z)\widetilde{G}(y,z)=G(y,z)-\bar{G}(z). We consider the Poisson equation for the Markov transition operator PP, with a zero-mean normalization:

𝒰−P​𝒰=G~,μ​𝒰=0.\mathcal{U}-P\mathcal{U}=\widetilde{G},\qquad\mu\mathcal{U}=0. (12)

Under Assumption A3, geometric mixing of the Markov input YkY_{k} gives the solution 𝒰⁡(⋅,z)=∑j≥0Pj​G~​(⋅,z)\mathcal{U}(\cdot,z)=\sum_{j\geq 0}P^{j}\widetilde{G}(\cdot,z) [9, Section 5].

Set ξk=G⁡(Yk,z⋆)\xi_{k}=G(Y_{k},z^{\star}) and ζk+1​(z)=𝒰⁡(Yk+1,z)−(P​𝒰)​(Yk,z)\zeta_{k+1}(z)=\mathcal{U}(Y_{k+1},z)-(P\mathcal{U})(Y_{k},z).

Lemma 1 (Long-run covariance).

Under Assumption A3, ζk+1​(z)\zeta_{k+1}(z) is a martingale difference for fixed zz, meaning 𝔼⁡[ζk+1​(z)∣ℱk]=0\mathbb{E}[\zeta_{k+1}(z)\mid\mathcal{F}_{k}]=0. For the stationary input chain Y0∼μY_{0}\sim\mu, write Kh=𝔼⁡[ξ0​ξh⊤]K_{h}=\mathbb{E}[\xi_{0}\xi_{h}^{\top}]. Then

Q\displaystyle Q =limm→∞m−1​𝔼​[(∑k=0m−1ξk)​(∑k=0m−1ξk)⊤]\displaystyle=\lim_{m\to\infty}m^{-1}\mathbb{E}\left[\Bigl(\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\xi_{k}\Bigr)\Bigl(\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\xi_{k}\Bigr)^{\top}\right] (13)
=K0+∑h≥1(Kh+Kh⊤)=𝔼⁡[ζ1​(z⋆)​ζ1​(z⋆)⊤].\displaystyle=K_{0}+\sum_{h\geq 1}(K_{h}+K_{h}^{\top})=\mathbb{E}[\zeta_{1}(z^{\star})\zeta_{1}(z^{\star})^{\top}].

The sum in (13) accumulates the equilibrium noise over mm steps. To compute its covariance per step, we use the Poisson equation to write

∑k=0m−1ξk\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\xi_{k} =∑k=0m−1ζk+1​(z⋆)+𝒰⁡(Y0,z⋆)−𝒰⁡(Ym,z⋆).\displaystyle=\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\zeta_{k+1}(z^{\star})+\mathcal{U}(Y_{0},z^{\star})-\mathcal{U}(Y_{m},z^{\star}).

The first term is a martingale sum. The remaining difference depends only on the initial and final noise states and is bounded uniformly in mm, since 𝖸\mathsf{Y} is finite. Its covariance and cross terms vanish after division by mm, yielding the last equality in (13); see Appendix C.2.

3.3 Covariance of Stationary Iterates

We now approximate Γη,ρ=Cov⁡(z−z⋆)\Gamma_{\eta,\rho}=\operatorname{Cov}(z-z^{\star}) under the stationary law πη,ρ\pi_{\eta,\rho}. This covariance measures fluctuations around the stationary mean and enters the bias expansion in Section 4.

Write Jρ=Dρ​JJ_{\rho}=D_{\rho}J, which is Hurwitz for sufficiently small ρ\rho by Proposition 1. Define Σρ\Sigma_{\rho} as the unique solution of the Lyapunov equation

Jρ​Σρ+Σρ​Jρ⊤+Dρ​Q​Dρ=0.J_{\rho}\Sigma_{\rho}+\Sigma_{\rho}J_{\rho}^{\top}+D_{\rho}QD_{\rho}=0. (14)

Appendix Lemma 5 derives this equation from the linearized recursion. The next proposition shows that η​Σρ\eta\Sigma_{\rho} approximates Γη,ρ\Gamma_{\eta,\rho}, the covariance of the joint iterates zk=(xk⊤,θk⊤)⊤z_{k}=(x_{k}^{\top},\theta_{k}^{\top})^{\top} generated by (3) under the stationary law πη,ρ\pi_{\eta,\rho}.

Proposition 2 (Uniform covariance approximation).

Under Assumptions A1–A5, for all sufficiently small positive η,ρ\eta,\rho,

Γη,ρ=η​Σρ+Rη,ρΓ,‖Rη,ρΓ‖≤C​η3/2.\Gamma_{\eta,\rho}=\eta\Sigma_{\rho}+R^{\Gamma}_{\eta,\rho},\qquad\|R^{\Gamma}_{\eta,\rho}\|\leq C\eta^{3/2}. (15)

The constant CC is independent of η\eta and ρ\rho, so the bound remains valid as ρ↓0\rho\downarrow 0.

Proof idea.

The complete proof of Proposition 2 is given in Appendix D.2. Apply the Poisson correction (90) and then the tangent transformation (6); the leading noise then has zero conditional mean. Stationarity then gives a covariance balance, with remainder terms controlled by the moment and regularity assumptions. Crucially, the remainder in the slow covariance equation carries a factor ρ\rho, offsetting its O⁡(1/ρ)O(1/\rho) relaxation time. Solving this balance and removing the correction gives the stated bound; see Appendix D.2. ∎

4 Stationary Mean Bias

We derive the stationary mean bias from the balance 𝔼​G​(Yk,zk)=0\mathbb{E}G(Y_{k},z_{k})=0. Theorem 1 combines the covariance approximation of Proposition 2, a second-order Taylor expansion of G¯​(z)\bar{G}(z) about z⋆z^{\star}, and a Poisson-corrector identity to obtain mη,ρ=η​b​(ρ)+O⁡(η3/2)m_{\eta,\rho}=\eta b(\rho)+O(\eta^{3/2}). The coefficient separates curvature and direct Markov contributions. Lemma 2 supplies the auxiliary bound ‖mη,ρ‖=O⁡(η)\|m_{\eta,\rho}\|=O(\eta) used in the theorem’s proof. Both bounds are uniform as ρ↓0\rho\downarrow 0.

Define the curvature map and direct Markov response by

𝒞​(M)i=12​Tr⁡(D2​G¯i​(z⋆)​M),\mathcal{C}(M)_{i}=\tfrac{1}{2}\operatorname{Tr}(D^{2}\bar{G}_{i}(z^{\star})M),
rρ=∑y,y′μ⁡(y)​P​(y,y′)​Dz​𝒰​(y′,z⋆)​Dρ​G​(y,z⋆).r_{\rho}=\sum_{y,y^{\prime}}\mu(y)P(y,y^{\prime})D_{z}\mathcal{U}(y^{\prime},z^{\star})D_{\rho}G(y,z^{\star}). (16)
Theorem 1 (Fixed-ratio bias).

If Assumptions A1–A5 hold,

mη,ρ=η​b​(ρ)+O⁡(η3/2),b⁡(ρ)=−J−1​{𝒞⁡(Σρ)+rρ},\begin{gathered}m_{\eta,\rho}=\eta b(\rho)+O(\eta^{3/2}),\\ b(\rho)=-J^{-1}\{\mathcal{C}(\Sigma_{\rho})+r_{\rho}\},\end{gathered} (17)

with a remainder uniform for 0<ρ≤ρ00<\rho\leq\rho_{0}.

Lemma 2 (A priori mean bound).

Under the same assumptions, ‖mη,ρ‖≤C​η\|m_{\eta,\rho}\|\leq C\eta uniformly.

The proof is given in Appendix D.3; Appendix D.4 supplies the detailed identities and remainder bounds.

5 Bias Expansion as the Step-Size Ratio Vanishes.

Section 4 leaves the ratio dependence implicit in b⁡(ρ)b(\rho). As ρ↓0\rho\downarrow 0, the slow relaxation rate vanishes on the fast clock, making the covariance equation singular at ρ=0\rho=0. We rescale the covariance blocks to obtain regular limiting equations and expand b⁡(ρ)b(\rho). Theorem 2 identifies contributions proportional to η\eta, ε\varepsilon, and ε2/η\varepsilon^{2}/\eta, with an O⁡(η3/2+ε3/η2)O(\eta^{3/2}+\varepsilon^{3}/\eta^{2}) remainder whose implied constant is independent of η\eta and ρ\rho. This expansion also guides bias reduction using runs at different step sizes. For example, at fixed ratio, halving both steps halves the leading bias, so twice the finer-step average minus the coarser-step average cancels that leading stationary bias. Section 6 adapts this cancellation to runs in which the step-size ratio also changes.

Theorem 2 (Singular expansion).

Under Assumptions A1–A5, uniformly for small positive η,ρ\eta,\rho,

mη,ρ\displaystyle m_{\eta,\rho} =η​b0+ε​b1+ε2η​b2+O⁡(η3/2+ε3η2).\displaystyle=\eta b_{0}+\varepsilon b_{1}+\frac{\varepsilon^{2}}{\eta}b_{2}+O\!\left(\eta^{3/2}+\frac{\varepsilon^{3}}{\eta^{2}}\right). (18)
Proof sketch.

In tangent coordinates, write

T​Σρ​T⊤=(U⁡(ρ)ρ​R​(ρ)ρ​R​(ρ)⊤ρ​V​(ρ)).T\Sigma_{\rho}T^{\top}=\begin{pmatrix}U(\rho)&\rho R(\rho)\\ \rho R(\rho)^{\top}&\rho V(\rho)\end{pmatrix}.

Rescaling the cross and slow covariance equations gives a linear system with polynomial coefficients in ρ\rho. At ρ=0\rho=0, it is triangular and invertible by Hurwitz stability of AA and SS. Its solution is therefore analytic near zero. Expanding Σρ\Sigma_{\rho} through order ρ2\rho^{2}, using the affine dependence of rρr_{\rho} on ρ\rho, and substituting into Theorem 1 gives the result. The detailed proof and coefficient formulas are in Appendix E.1. ∎

In tangent coordinates, the leading fast covariance, fast–slow cross-covariance, and slow covariance are η​U​(ρ)=O⁡(η)\eta U(\rho)=O(\eta), η​ρ​R​(ρ)=O⁡(ε)\eta\rho R(\rho)=O(\varepsilon), and η​ρ​V​(ρ)=O⁡(ε)\eta\rho V(\rho)=O(\varepsilon), respectively. The absolute O⁡(η3/2)O(\eta^{3/2}) covariance remainder can obscure the O⁡(ε)O(\varepsilon) terms when ρ≲η\rho\lesssim\sqrt{\eta}. The sharper O⁡(ε)O(\varepsilon) bounds for the actual slow covariance and fast–slow cross-covariance are additional conditions collected in Assumption A7. They are not needed for Proposition 2 or Theorems 1–2. Proposition 4 gives sufficient conditions under which these stronger bounds hold.

6 Extrapolation Along Step-Size Paths

Time averaging reduces random fluctuations but does not remove stationary bias. We reduce this bias by combining averages from several runs at different pairs of fast and slow step sizes. For each run, we choose a fast step η\eta and set the slow step to ε=ηp\varepsilon=\eta^{p}, with the same fixed p>1p>1 across runs. Thus, reducing η\eta also determines how ε\varepsilon decreases. This relation between the two step sizes defines the step-size path. The expansion in Section 5 describes how the bias changes along this path, allowing us to choose weights so that the leading stationary bias terms cancel. Proposition 3 gives a three-run combination that cancels the contributions proportional to the fast and slow steps. We also describe how to cancel further terms and bound the remaining bias.

Before choosing extrapolation weights, we identify the bias powers along the chosen step-size path and compare them with the remainder. For ε=ηp\varepsilon=\eta^{p}, p>1p>1, Theorem 2 gives

m⁡(η)=η​b0+ηp​b1+η2​p−1​b2+O⁡(η3/2+η3​p−2).m(\eta)=\eta b_{0}+\eta^{p}b_{1}+\eta^{2p-1}b_{2}+O(\eta^{3/2}+\eta^{3p-2}). (19)

A nonzero bias term can be distinguished from the remainder when it decays more slowly as η↓0\eta\downarrow 0. Since 3​p−2>2​p−1>p>13p-2>2p-1>p>1, comparison with the O⁡(η3/2)O(\eta^{3/2}) remainder determines which displayed terms satisfy this condition: ηp​b1\eta^{p}b_{1} does so for 1<p<3/21<p<3/2, and η2​p−1​b2\eta^{2p-1}b_{2} for 1<p<5/41<p<5/4. Under the additional additive-i.i.d. conditions of Theorem 4, the sharper O⁡(η2)O(\eta^{2}) remainder extends the latter range to 1<p<3/21<p<3/2.

At fixed ρ\rho, let Mρ​(h)M_{\rho}(h) denote the stationary mean at steps (η,ε)=(h,ρ​h)(\eta,\varepsilon)=(h,\rho h). Halving both steps halves the leading bias, so twice the finer-step mean minus the coarser-step mean cancels this contribution:

2​Mρ​(h/2)−Mρ​(h)=z⋆+O⁡(h3/2).2M_{\rho}(h/2)-M_{\rho}(h)=z^{\star}+O(h^{3/2}). (20)

Along ε=ηp\varepsilon=\eta^{p}, reducing the fast step must preserve this relation: the corresponding pairs are (ηj,εj)=(2−j​h,(2−j​h)p)(\eta_{j},\varepsilon_{j})=(2^{-j}h,(2^{-j}h)^{p}). The bias terms proportional to hh and hph^{p} now decrease by different factors between successive runs. Proposition 3 gives weights for combining the three stationary means at j=0,1,2j=0,1,2 so that both terms cancel, and bounds the remaining bias.

Proposition 3 (Three-level path extrapolation).

Let M⁡(h)M(h) be the stationary mean at (h,hp)(h,h^{p}) under Theorem 2. Set q1=2−1q_{1}=2^{-1}, qp=2−pq_{p}=2^{-p}, and

(w0,w1,w2)=(q1​qp,−q1−qp,1)(1−q1)​(1−qp).(w_{0},w_{1},w_{2})=\frac{(q_{1}q_{p},-q_{1}-q_{p},1)}{(1-q_{1})(1-q_{p})}. (21)

Then

∑j=02wj​M​(2−j​h)=z⋆+O⁡(hmin⁡{2​p−1,3/2}).\sum_{j=0}^{2}w_{j}M(2^{-j}h)=z^{\star}+O\!\left(h^{\min\{2p-1,3/2\}}\right).

If the stationary weak remainder is O⁡(h2)O(h^{2}), replace 3/23/2 by 22.

Proof.

The weights satisfy ∑jwj=1\sum_{j}w_{j}=1, ∑jwj​2−j=0\sum_{j}w_{j}2^{-j}=0, and ∑jwj​2−j​p=0\sum_{j}w_{j}2^{-jp}=0. Apply these identities to (19). ∎

Appendix E gives weights for canceling additional bias terms and explains the limits imposed by the available remainder bounds. Extrapolation can increase sampling variance, so reducing bias does not necessarily improve accuracy at fixed computational cost.

An exactly solvable nonlinear Markov example in Appendix H verifies that the mixed bias term can be nonzero and illustrates these extrapolation rules using exact stationary means.

7 Finite-Time Consequences

A stationary coupling decomposes the error into initialization, centered fluctuation, and stationary mean. Under Assumptions A1–A5 and the additional block localization in Assumption A7,

𝔼​‖u‖2=O⁡(η),𝔼​‖v‖2=O⁡(ε+η2).\mathbb{E}\|u\|^{2}=O(\eta),\qquad\mathbb{E}\|v\|^{2}=O(\varepsilon+\eta^{2}). (22)

The η2\eta^{2} term is squared bias and can dominate the slow variance on thin paths.

Assumption A6 (Two-clock coupling).

A coupling with a stationary version satisfies

𝔼​‖zk−zkst‖≤C​{1+V⁡(z0)}​(e−c​η​k+e−c​ε​k),\mathbb{E}\|z_{k}-z_{k}^{\rm st}\|\leq C\{1+V(z_{0})\}(e^{-c\eta k}+e^{-c\varepsilon k}), (23)

where V≥0V\geq 0 has uniformly bounded invariant expectation. Any meeting-time contribution from different input initializations is included in this bound.

This additional condition does not follow from local linear stability.

Theorem 3 (Tail-average bias and initialization).

For z¯K,N=L−1​∑k=KN−1zk\bar{z}_{K,N}=L^{-1}\sum_{k=K}^{N-1}z_{k}, L=N−K>0L=N-K>0, under Assumption A6,

∥𝖳K,N∥≤C{1+V(z0)}[\displaystyle\|\mathsf{T}_{K,N}\|\leq C\{1+V(z_{0})\}\bigl[ e−c​η​Kmin{1,(ηL)−1}+e−c​ε​Kmin{1,(εL)−1}],\displaystyle e^{-c\eta K}\min\{1,(\eta L)^{-1}\}+e^{-c\varepsilon K}\min\{1,(\varepsilon L)^{-1}\}\bigr], (24)

where 𝖳K,N=𝔼​z¯K,N−𝔼​zst\mathsf{T}_{K,N}=\mathbb{E}\bar{z}_{K,N}-\mathbb{E}z^{\rm st}. If Assumptions A1–A5 also hold, then

𝔼​z¯K,N−z⋆=η​b​(ρ)+O⁡(η3/2)+𝖳K,N.\mathbb{E}\bar{z}_{K,N}-z^{\star}=\eta b(\rho)+O(\eta^{3/2})+\mathsf{T}_{K,N}. (25)
Proof.

Average (23) and use, for h=η,εh=\eta,\varepsilon,

L−1​∑k=KN−1e−c​h​k\displaystyle L^{-1}\sum_{k=K}^{N-1}e^{-chk} =e−c​h​K​1−e−c​h​LL⁡(1−e−c​h)\displaystyle=e^{-chK}\frac{1-e^{-chL}}{L(1-e^{-ch})}
≤C​e−c​h​K​min⁡{1,(h​L)−1}.\displaystyle\leq Ce^{-chK}\min\{1,(hL)^{-1}\}.

Then apply Theorem 1. ∎

Stationary initialization makes 𝖳K,N=0\mathsf{T}_{K,N}=0. For finite-run extrapolation, weighted initialization errors must lie below the retained remainder. Appendix I derives conditional blockwise mean-square bounds under additional stationary moment and coordinate L2L^{2} coupling assumptions.

8 Application: temporal-difference learning

We study fixed-policy value estimation using temporal-difference learning with gradient correction (TDC) [20, 16]. We compare stationary-bias predictions with simulations and evaluate extrapolation at equal update budgets.

8.1 Setup and Recursion

Let SkS_{k} be the state at time kk under a fixed policy, Rk+1R_{k+1} the reward on the transition to Sk+1S_{k+1}, and γ∈(0,1)\gamma\in(0,1) the discount factor. For a fixed scalar feature ϕ⁡(s)\phi(s), we approximate the discounted value function by Vθ​(s)=ϕ⁡(s)​θV_{\theta}(s)=\phi(s)\theta, with parameter θ∈ℝ\theta\in\mathbb{R}. Write ϕk=ϕ⁡(Sk)\phi_{k}=\phi(S_{k}) and define

δk=Rk+1+γ​ϕk+1​θk−ϕk​θk.\delta_{k}=R_{k+1}+\gamma\phi_{k+1}\theta_{k}-\phi_{k}\theta_{k}.

TDC uses a fast auxiliary variable wkw_{k} and a slow value parameter θk\theta_{k} [20]:

wk+1\displaystyle w_{k+1} =wk+η⁡(δk−ϕk​wk)​ϕk,\displaystyle=w_{k}+\eta(\delta_{k}-\phi_{k}w_{k})\phi_{k},
θk+1\displaystyle\theta_{k+1} =θk+ε⁡[δk​ϕk−γ​ϕk+1​ϕk​wk].\displaystyle=\theta_{k}+\varepsilon\bigl[\delta_{k}\phi_{k}-\gamma\phi_{k+1}\phi_{k}w_{k}\bigr].

Both updates use the current parameters and the same observed transition.

We use a Markov reward process with state space 𝖲={0,1,2,3,4}\mathsf{S}=\{0,1,2,3,4\}, representing positions along a five-site chain. From an interior state s∈{1,2,3}s\in\{1,2,3\}, the process stays at ss with probability 1/21/2 and moves to each neighboring state with probability 1/41/4. At either boundary, an attempted outward move becomes a self-loop: the process stays with probability 3/43/4 and moves to its only neighbor with probability 1/41/4. The reward is Rk+1=𝟏{Sk+1=4}R_{k+1}=\mathbf{1}\{S_{k+1}=4\}, so a transition earns reward one exactly when its destination is the rightmost state. The process continues after receiving this reward; state 44 is not terminal. We set ϕ⁡(s)=1+0.05​s\phi(s)=1+0.05s and γ=0.2\gamma=0.2. Our estimation target is the TD equilibrium θ⋆≈0.2443164284\theta^{\star}\approx 0.2443164284, derived in Appendix J.1. The updates are affine, so their curvature contribution vanishes; this example tests the direct Markov contribution to stationary bias.

8.2 Empirical Bias Estimation and Extrapolation

Our experiments have two goals: to compare the bias estimated from simulated trajectories with the theoretical bias expansion, and to assess whether extrapolation improves estimation accuracy at equal total update budgets.

Estimating bias from simulated trajectories.

Fix the step sizes η\eta and ε=η​ρ\varepsilon=\eta\rho. We generate R=256R=256 independent replications of the TDC recursion. In replication rr, we discard the first KK updates and average the next LL slow iterates:

θ^(r)=1L​∑ℓ=1LθK+ℓ(r).\widehat{\theta}^{(r)}=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{\ell=1}^{L}\theta^{(r)}_{K+\ell}.

The empirical bias is

B^η,ρθ=1R​∑r=1R(θ^(r)−θ⋆).\widehat{B}^{\theta}_{\eta,\rho}=\frac{1}{R}\sum_{r=1}^{R}\bigl(\widehat{\theta}^{(r)}-\theta^{\star}\bigr). (26)

The target θ⋆\theta^{\star} is the equilibrium of the averaged TD problem, given in (224). Thus, the empirical bias is calculated directly from simulated iterates and the known target. For finite KK and LL, this estimates the bias of the post-burn average. We interpret it as an estimate of stationary bias when the remaining initialization effect is negligible.

Comparison with the theoretical prediction.

Theorem 1, specialized to this affine TDC recursion in Appendix J.1, gives, for sufficiently small positive η\eta and ρ\rho,

Bη,ρθ:=𝔼πη,ρ​[θ]−θ⋆=η⁡(b0θ+ρ​b1θ)+O⁡(η3/2).B^{\theta}_{\eta,\rho}:=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\eta,\rho}}[\theta]-\theta^{\star}=\eta\bigl(b_{0}^{\theta}+\rho b_{1}^{\theta}\bigr)+O(\eta^{3/2}).

Consequently, at a fixed ratio ρ\rho, the normalized empirical bias B^η,ρθ/η\widehat{B}^{\theta}_{\eta,\rho}/\eta can be compared with the leading coefficient b0θ+ρ​b1θb_{0}^{\theta}+\rho b_{1}^{\theta}. The top panels of Figure 1 show this comparison at ρ∈{0.1,0.25}\rho\in\{0.1,0.25\}. The points and their confidence intervals are obtained from simulations; the dashed horizontal lines mark b0θ+ρ​b1θb_{0}^{\theta}+\rho b_{1}^{\theta}, the predicted limit of the normalized stationary bias Bη,ρθ/ηB^{\theta}_{\eta,\rho}/\eta as η→0\eta\to 0 at fixed ρ\rho.

As a control, we independently sample transition pairs from the same stationary transition distribution. This preserves the averaged TD problem and its target θ⋆\theta^{\star} while removing serial dependence. The stationary bias of this independent-pair recursion is zero. Comparing its empirical bias with that of the Markov recursion therefore examines the effect of temporal dependence.

Extrapolation at equal update budgets.

We compare ordinary averaging with extrapolated estimates along the step-size path

ηj=h​2−j,εj=ηjp,h=0.05,p=6/5.\eta_{j}=h2^{-j},\qquad\varepsilon_{j}=\eta_{j}^{p},\qquad h=0.05,\quad p=6/5.

Within each replication, let θ^j\widehat{\theta}_{j} denote the post-burn average at level jj. Ordinary averaging uses level 00. The two-level rule RR {1}\{1\} uses

θ^RR​{1}=2​θ^1−θ^0.\widehat{\theta}_{\mathrm{RR}\{1\}}=2\widehat{\theta}_{1}-\widehat{\theta}_{0}.

The three-level rules RR {1,2}\{1,2\} and RR {1,p}\{1,p\} use weights that sum to one and cancel the indicated powers of hh.

We use total update budgets B∈{217,219,221}B\in\{2^{17},2^{19},2^{21}\}. A method with mm levels allocates N=⌊B/m⌋N=\lfloor B/m\rfloor updates to each level, including burn-in. Within a replication, the levels share the same input sequence. Each replication produces one estimate for each method. We compute empirical bias, standard deviation, and RMSE across these independent replication-level estimates. The bottom panels of Figure 1 show empirical bias and standard deviation. RMSE measures their combined contribution to estimation error.

Appendix J.1 verifies the assumptions and derives the theoretical bias coefficients. Appendix J.2 specifies the simulation lengths, burn-in, and uncertainty calculations. The nonlinear mixed bias term is illustrated separately in Appendix H.

9 Conclusion

For nonlinear two-timescale stochastic approximation, we derive a stationary-bias expansion with terms η​b0+ε​b1+(ε2/η)​b2\eta b_{0}+\varepsilon b_{1}+(\varepsilon^{2}/\eta)b_{2} and uniform remainder control as the step-size ratio vanishes. Along paths ε=ηp\varepsilon=\eta^{p}, these contributions have powers 11, pp, and 2​p−12p-1, motivating Richardson–Romberg extrapolation rules adapted to the chosen path. The TDC experiments illustrate the practical trade-off: cancelling additional bias terms can increase sampling variability, so higher-order cancellation need not improve accuracy at equal update budgets. Sharper Markov remainder bounds and optimal allocation across extrapolation levels remain open questions.

We first recall the notation and the assumptions from the main paper. The general proofs come next, followed by the additive-noise refinement, a sufficient localization condition, the worked example, finite-time consequences, and the temporal-difference learning application and additional experiments.

A.1 The Algorithm and Its Two Clocks

The fast variable is xk∈ℝdxx_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}} and the slow variable is θk∈ℝdθ\theta_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\theta}}. They evolve according to

xk+1\displaystyle x_{k+1} =xk+η​H​(Yk,xk,θk),\displaystyle=x_{k}+\eta H(Y_{k},x_{k},\theta_{k}), (27)
θk+1\displaystyle\theta_{k+1} =θk+ε​F​(Yk,xk,θk).\displaystyle=\theta_{k}+\varepsilon F(Y_{k},x_{k},\theta_{k}). (28)

Here η>0\eta>0 is the fast step size, ε>0\varepsilon>0 is the slow step size, HH and FF are the two update fields, and YkY_{k} is the random input. The state space is Euclidean; no projection is applied after either update. A stationary analysis therefore needs a global stability condition ().

The random input is an exogenous Markov chain on a finite state space 𝖸\mathsf{Y} with PP as its transition matrix. We assume that this chain has a unique stationary distribution μ\mu and mixes geometrically.

The ratio

ρ=εη\rho=\frac{\varepsilon}{\eta} (29)

measures how much the slow variable moves during one unit of fast algorithmic time. We work with 0<ρ≤ρ00<\rho\leq\rho_{0}, where ρ0\rho_{0} is a sufficiently small fixed constant. Equivalently, ε=η​ρ\varepsilon=\eta\rho.

The limit η→0\eta\to 0 controls the size of the stationary fluctuations; the limit ρ→0\rho\to 0 separates the two clocks:

fast time tk=kη,slow time sk=kε=ρtk.\boxed{\text{fast time }t_{k}=k\eta,\qquad\text{slow time }s_{k}=k\varepsilon=\rho t_{k}.} (30)

We distinguish two limiting regimes. In the fixed-ratio regime, η→0\eta\to 0 while ρ=ε/η\rho=\varepsilon/\eta remains fixed and positive, so ε=ρ​η→0\varepsilon=\rho\eta\to 0. In the singular-ratio regime, both η→0\eta\to 0 and ρ→0\rho\to 0, so ε=o⁡(η)\varepsilon=o(\eta) and the two clocks become increasingly separated. A result established separately for each fixed ρ\rho need not hold uniformly in the singular-ratio regime, because its bounds may deteriorate as ρ→0\rho\to 0. The uniform remainder bounds proved below ensure that our stationary expansion also applies in the singular-ratio regime.

A.2 Averaged Dynamics and the Fast Equilibrium Manifold

This subsection introduces the averaged dynamics and the fast equilibrium manifold, and gives a high-level interpretation of their fast–slow structure. The qualitative discussion of relaxation and tracking motivates the coordinates introduced in the next subsection. The local ODE geometry and quantitative two-clock semigroup bounds are developed in Appendix B.

The stationary distribution μ\mu of the exogenous chain defines the averaged update fields

H¯​(x,θ)\displaystyle\bar{H}(x,\theta) =∑y∈𝖸μ⁡(y)​H​(y,x,θ),\displaystyle=\sum_{y\in\mathsf{Y}}\mu(y)H(y,x,\theta), (31)
F¯​(x,θ)\displaystyle\bar{F}(x,\theta) =∑y∈𝖸μ⁡(y)​F​(y,x,θ).\displaystyle=\sum_{y\in\mathsf{Y}}\mu(y)F(y,x,\theta). (32)

These fields describe the deterministic motion obtained after averaging the rapid random fluctuations of YkY_{k}.

On the fast time scale t=k​ηt=k\eta, the formal averaged ODE is

d​xd​t\displaystyle\frac{dx}{dt} =H¯​(x,θ),\displaystyle=\bar{H}(x,\theta), (33)
d​θd​t\displaystyle\frac{d\theta}{dt} =ρ​F¯​(x,θ).\displaystyle=\rho\,\bar{F}(x,\theta). (34)

When ρ\rho is small, θ\theta barely changes while the fast ODE relaxes. This suggests freezing θ\theta and studying

d​xd​t=H¯​(x,θ).\frac{dx}{dt}=\bar{H}(x,\theta). (35)

Assume that, for every θ\theta in the region of interest, this frozen ODE has a locally unique asymptotically stable equilibrium. Denote it by λ⁡(θ)\lambda(\theta), so

H¯​(λ​(θ),θ)=0.\bar{H}(\lambda(\theta),\theta)=0. (36)

The graph x=λ⁡(θ)x=\lambda(\theta) is the fast equilibrium manifold. After the fast transient has died away, the pair (x,θ)(x,\theta) should remain close to this graph while θ\theta evolves.

Substituting x=λ⁡(θ)x=\lambda(\theta) into the averaged slow update gives the reduced slow field

g⁡(θ)=F¯​(λ⁡(θ),θ).g(\theta)=\bar{F}(\lambda(\theta),\theta). (37)

On slow time s=k​εs=k\varepsilon, the reduced ODE is

d​θd​s=g⁡(θ).\frac{d\theta}{ds}=g(\theta). (38)

Let θ⋆\theta^{\star} be its stable equilibrium, so that g⁡(θ⋆)=0g(\theta^{\star})=0. The corresponding equilibrium of the full averaged system is

x⋆=λ⁡(θ⋆),z⋆=(x⋆θ⋆).x^{\star}=\lambda(\theta^{\star}),\qquad z^{\star}=\begin{pmatrix}x^{\star}\\ \theta^{\star}\end{pmatrix}. (39)

For vector-valued variables, local stability is expressed through the Jacobians

A=Dx​H¯​(x⋆,θ⋆),S=Dθ​g​(θ⋆).A=D_{x}\bar{H}(x^{\star},\theta^{\star}),\qquad S=D_{\theta}g(\theta^{\star}). (40)

We assume that both AA and SS are Hurwitz: every eigenvalue has strictly negative real part. For initial conditions sufficiently close to the relevant equilibrium, this gives bounds of the form C​e−c​tCe^{-ct} times the initial displacement for the frozen fast ODE, and C​e−c​sCe^{-cs} times the initial displacement for the reduced slow ODE, with suitable constants C,c>0C,c>0. Thus both deterministic systems approach their equilibria at an exponential rate, measured on their respective time scales t=k​ηt=k\eta and s=k​εs=k\varepsilon. We call this exponential approach toward equilibrium exponential relaxation, and use relaxation as shorthand below. Local Hurwitz stability does not ensure an invariant law for the unprojected stochastic recursion; global localization is imposed in .

A.3 Coordinates Relative to the Fast Equilibrium Manifold

The raw error x−x⋆x-x^{\star} combines two effects: displacement away from the fast manifold and movement of the manifold caused by θ−θ⋆\theta-\theta^{\star}. It is more informative to introduce

u^=x−λ⁡(θ),v=θ−θ⋆.\widehat{u}=x-\lambda(\theta),\qquad v=\theta-\theta^{\star}. (41)

These coordinates are initially defined where the local map λ\lambda is available. The variable u^\widehat{u} measures displacement from the moving fast equilibrium, while vv measures slow displacement. Their use throughout the stationary law requires the extension specified in Assumption A7.

One update shows why this coordinate is useful. Let x+=x+η​H​(Y,x,θ)x^{+}=x+\eta H(Y,x,\theta) and θ+=θ+ε​F​(Y,x,θ)\theta^{+}=\theta+\varepsilon F(Y,x,\theta). When the segment [θ,θ+][\theta,\theta^{+}] lies in the domain of the chosen C2C^{2} map λ\lambda, we have

u^+\displaystyle\widehat{u}^{+} =x+−λ⁡(θ+)\displaystyle=x^{+}-\lambda(\theta^{+})
=u^+η​H​(Y,x,θ)−{λ⁡(θ+ε​F​(Y,x,θ))−λ⁡(θ)}.\displaystyle=\widehat{u}+\eta H(Y,x,\theta)-\{\lambda(\theta+\varepsilon F(Y,x,\theta))-\lambda(\theta)\}. (42)

For λ:ℝdθ→ℝdx\lambda:\mathbb{R}^{d_{\theta}}\to\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}}, the Jacobian with respect to θ\theta has dimensions

Dθ​λ​(θ)∈ℝdx×dθ,Dθ​λ​(θ)​F​(Y,x,θ)∈ℝdx.D_{\theta}\lambda(\theta)\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}\times d_{\theta}},\qquad D_{\theta}\lambda(\theta)F(Y,x,\theta)\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}}.

If λ\lambda has a locally Lipschitz derivative (in particular, if λ∈C2\lambda\in C^{2}), Taylor expansion gives

λ⁡(θ+ε​F)−λ⁡(θ)=ε​Dθ​λ​(θ)​F+O⁡(ε2​‖F‖2).\lambda(\theta+\varepsilon F)-\lambda(\theta)=\varepsilon D_{\theta}\lambda(\theta)F+O(\varepsilon^{2}\|F\|^{2}).

Using ε=η​ρ\varepsilon=\eta\rho yields

u^+\displaystyle\widehat{u}^{+} =u^+η⁡[H⁡(Y,x,θ)−ρ​Dθ​λ​(θ)​F​(Y,x,θ)]+O⁡(ε2​‖F⁡(Y,x,θ)‖2).\displaystyle=\widehat{u}+\eta\bigl[H(Y,x,\theta)-\rho D_{\theta}\lambda(\theta)F(Y,x,\theta)\bigr]+O(\varepsilon^{2}\|F(Y,x,\theta)\|^{2}). (43)

The factor ρ=ε/η\rho=\varepsilon/\eta is now visible in front of the slow forcing of the fast-manifold error. This factor must be retained. A generic bound for the stacked recursion can replace the two relaxation rates by the slow spectral gap, producing a spurious factor 1/ρ1/\rho. In the coordinate (u^,v)(\widehat{u},v), slow forcing has size ρ\rho and acts over a relaxation time of order 1/ρ1/\rho on the fast clock; the two factors compensate.

Near z⋆z^{\star}, reserve uu for the linear approximation of the nonlinear tracking error:

u=(x−x⋆)−Dθ​λ​(θ⋆)​(θ−θ⋆)and henceu^=u+O⁡(‖θ−θ⋆‖2).u=(x-x^{\star})-D_{\theta}\lambda(\theta^{\star})(\theta-\theta^{\star})\qquad\text{and hence}\qquad\widehat{u}=u+O(\|\theta-\theta^{\star}\|^{2}). (44)

To show that the difference between u^\widehat{u} and its linear approximation uu is O⁡(‖θ−θ⋆‖2)O(\|\theta-\theta^{\star}\|^{2}), let δ​x=x−x⋆\delta x=x-x^{\star}, v=θ−θ⋆v=\theta-\theta^{\star}, and Λ=Dθ​λ​(θ⋆)\Lambda=D_{\theta}\lambda(\theta^{\star}). Since x⋆=λ⁡(θ⋆)x^{\star}=\lambda(\theta^{\star}), the C2C^{2} Taylor formula is

λ⁡(θ⋆+v)=x⋆+Λ​v+rλ​(v),rλ​(v)=∫01(1−s)​Dθ2​λ​(θ⋆+s​v)​[v,v]​𝑑s.\lambda(\theta^{\star}+v)=x^{\star}+\Lambda v+r_{\lambda}(v),\qquad r_{\lambda}(v)=\int_{0}^{1}(1-s)D_{\theta}^{2}\lambda(\theta^{\star}+sv)[v,v]\,ds.

A bound ‖Dθ2​λ‖≤M\|D_{\theta}^{2}\lambda\|\leq M along the segment gives ‖rλ​(v)‖≤(M/2)​‖v‖2\|r_{\lambda}(v)\|\leq(M/2)\|v\|^{2}. Therefore

u^=x−λ⁡(θ)=δ​x−Λ​v−rλ​(v)=u−rλ​(v).\widehat{u}=x-\lambda(\theta)=\delta x-\Lambda v-r_{\lambda}(v)=u-r_{\lambda}(v).

This proves equation 44 in vector norm; the minus sign is absorbed by the big-OO notation. Differentiability alone would give only u^=u+o⁡(‖v‖)\widehat{u}=u+o(\|v\|). The nonlinear version is useful for localization and transient estimates; the linearized version is convenient when computing covariance and bias coefficients.

A.4 Compact Notation

Define the stacked state and update

z=(xθ),G⁡(y,z)=(H⁡(y,x,θ)F⁡(y,x,θ)),z=\begin{pmatrix}x\\ \theta\end{pmatrix},\qquad G(y,z)=\begin{pmatrix}H(y,x,\theta)\\ F(y,x,\theta)\end{pmatrix}, (45)

and define the block scaling matrix

Dρ=(Idx00ρ​Idθ).D_{\rho}=\begin{pmatrix}I_{d_{x}}&0\\ 0&\rho I_{d_{\theta}}\end{pmatrix}. (46)

Here IdxI_{d_{x}} and IdθI_{d_{\theta}} are identity matrices of dimensions dxd_{x} and dθd_{\theta}. The recursions in equations 27 and 28 are then exactly equivalent to

zk+1=zk+η​Dρ​G​(Yk,zk).z_{k+1}=z_{k}+\eta D_{\rho}G(Y_{k},z_{k}). (47)

The lower block has the smaller step η​ρ=ε\eta\rho=\varepsilon.

A.5 Standing Assumptions

The core stationary assumptions are stated in Section 2.2; the additional coupling and block conditions are stated separately.

Assumptions A1 and A2.

Local smoothness and Hurwitz stability specify the deterministic geometry and the fixed tangent transformation.

Assumption A3.

The exogenous finite-state chain satisfies the stated Doeblin condition.

Assumption A4.

A selected family of joint invariant laws satisfies 𝔼​‖z−z⋆‖4≤C​η2\mathbb{E}\|z-z^{\star}\|^{4}\leq C\eta^{2}, uniformly in the step sizes.

Assumption A5.

The update fields have globally bounded first and second derivatives. Lemma 4 derives the expected Taylor and Poisson-corrector bounds from these conditions.

Assumption A6.

The L1L^{1} coupling controls initialization of expected tail averages. The blockwise mean-square statements additionally require the coordinate L2L^{2} coupling bounds and the uniform stationary V2V_{2} moment displayed in Appendix I.

Assumption A7.

The stronger raw and centered block moments, tangent cross-covariance bound, and stationary extension and remainder conditions for λ\lambda support supplementary blockwise fluctuation statements. They are not assumptions of the core covariance and bias expansions.

The local deterministic and Markov assumptions determine the coefficients; fourth-moment localization and update regularity justify the stationary expansions. Additional block conditions and coupling are invoked only for the conclusions that use them.

A.6 Quantities of Interest and Step-Size Regimes

Suppose that for sufficiently small (η,ρ)(\eta,\rho) the joint chain (Yk,zk)(Y_{k},z_{k}) admits an invariant law, denoted by πη,ρ\pi_{\eta,\rho}. The stationary mean displacement from the averaged equilibrium is

mη,ρ=𝔼πη,ρ​[z]−z⋆.m_{\eta,\rho}=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\eta,\rho}}[z]-z^{\star}. (48)

The centered stationary covariance is

Γη,ρ=𝔼πη,ρ​[(z−𝔼πη,ρ​z)​(z−𝔼πη,ρ​z)⊤].\Gamma_{\eta,\rho}=\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\eta,\rho}}\left[(z-\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\eta,\rho}}z)(z-\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\eta,\rho}}z)^{\top}\right]. (49)

The superscript ⊤\top denotes matrix transpose. The corresponding mean-square distance decomposes as

𝔼πη,ρ​‖z−z⋆‖2=tr⁡(Γη,ρ)+‖mη,ρ‖2,\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\eta,\rho}}\|z-z^{\star}\|^{2}=\operatorname{tr}(\Gamma_{\eta,\rho})+\|m_{\eta,\rho}\|^{2}, (50)

where tr\operatorname{tr} is the matrix trace and ∥⋅∥\|\cdot\| is the Euclidean norm. Finite-time concentration, stationary covariance, and stationary bias expansions thus address distinct properties of the recursion.

For a trajectory started from an arbitrary initial condition, let K≥0K\geq 0 be the burn-in length and let N>KN>K. We average the iterates zK,…,zN−1z_{K},\ldots,z_{N-1}, so the averaging window contains L=N−KL=N-K iterates. The tail average is

z¯K,N=1L​∑k=KN−1zk.\bar{z}_{K,N}=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{k=K}^{N-1}z_{k}. (51)

Let ν\nu denote the initial law of the joint chain. Adding and subtracting the invariant mean gives the exact decomposition

𝔼ν​[z¯K,N]−z⋆\displaystyle\mathbb{E}_{\nu}[\bar{z}_{K,N}]-z^{\star} =mη,ρ+𝖳K,N​(ν),\displaystyle=m_{\eta,\rho}+\mathsf{T}_{K,N}(\nu),
𝖳K,N​(ν)\displaystyle\mathsf{T}_{K,N}(\nu) :=1L​∑k=KN−1(𝔼ν​[zk]−𝔼πη,ρ​[z]).\displaystyle:=\frac{1}{L}\sum_{k=K}^{N-1}\bigl(\mathbb{E}_{\nu}[z_{k}]-\mathbb{E}_{\pi_{\eta,\rho}}[z]\bigr).

The first term is the persistent stationary displacement. Under stationary initialization, 𝖳K,N=0\mathsf{T}_{K,N}=0 for every K,NK,N; averaging reduces sampling variability but leaves the mean displacement unchanged. The second term is the initialization transient. To bound the initialization transient 𝖳K,N​(ν)\mathsf{T}_{K,N}(\nu), we need an estimate of how quickly the expected iterates approach the stationary mean. Theorem 3 bounds this contribution under the two-clock coupling assumption.

The ratio ρ\rho determines the form of the persistent displacement. Fixed-ratio analysis holds ρ∈(0,ρ0]\rho\in(0,\rho_{0}] fixed and lets η↓0\eta\downarrow 0 with ε=ρ​η\varepsilon=\rho\eta, giving a representation

mη,ρ=η​b​(ρ)+Rη,ρ.m_{\eta,\rho}=\eta b(\rho)+R_{\eta,\rho}.

Singular-ratio analysis also lets ρ↓0\rho\downarrow 0. At ρ=0\rho=0 the slow block of DρD_{\rho} vanishes, the slow equation freezes, and its spectral gap collapses. A remainder bound at each fixed ρ\rho need not be uniform in this limit.

Appendix E develops the ratio expansion and explains how its powers determine the extrapolation weights.

Appendix B ODE geometry of two timescales

This section explains how coordinates relative to the fast equilibrium manifold separate fast tracking from slow evolution. As ρ→0\rho\to 0, slow relaxation takes increasingly long on the fast clock. We therefore keep the two relaxation rates and the factors of ρ\rho in the coupling terms explicit.

We first derive the exact coordinate dynamics for both the averaged ODE and the discrete recursion (Subsection B.1). We then linearize at the equilibrium to identify the fast and reduced slow Jacobian blocks (Subsection B.2). This linear structure leads to bounds that retain both relaxation rates, with constants independent of sufficiently small positive ρ\rho (Subsection B.3). These deterministic calculations provide tools for the stationary covariance and bias proofs developed later; stationary existence and localization require additional assumptions.

B.1 Exact Fast-Manifold Dynamics

We use the clocks (30), the fast equilibrium graph (36), the reduced field (37), and the fast-manifold coordinates (u^,v)(\widehat{u},v) of (41), and derive the dynamics in these coordinates.

To distinguish the exact coordinate u^\widehat{u} from its tangent approximation uu, use a neutral dummy variable w∈ℝdxw\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}} and define

h⁡(w,v)\displaystyle h(w,v) =H¯​(λ⁡(θ⋆+v)+w,θ⋆+v),\displaystyle=\bar{H}\bigl(\lambda(\theta^{\star}+v)+w,\theta^{\star}+v\bigr), (52)
f⁡(w,v)\displaystyle f(w,v) =F¯​(λ⁡(θ⋆+v)+w,θ⋆+v),\displaystyle=\bar{F}\bigl(\lambda(\theta^{\star}+v)+w,\theta^{\star}+v\bigr), (53)
ℓ⁡(v)\displaystyle\ell(v) =Dθ​λ​(θ⋆+v)∈ℝdx×dθ.\displaystyle=D_{\theta}\lambda(\theta^{\star}+v)\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}\times d_{\theta}}. (54)

Here ℓ⁡(v)\ell(v) is the Jacobian of λ\lambda with respect to θ\theta (equivalently, with respect to vv); it is not a time derivative. At the actual state w=u^w=\widehat{u}, since x=λ⁡(θ⋆+v)+u^x=\lambda(\theta^{\star}+v)+\widehat{u}. The chain rule applied to the fast-clock ODE equations 33 and 34 gives the exact fast-clock equations

u^˙=h⁡(u^,v)−ρ​ℓ​(v)​f​(u^,v),v˙=ρ​f​(u^,v).\dot{\widehat{u}}=h(\widehat{u},v)-\rho\ell(v)f(\widehat{u},v),\qquad\dot{v}=\rho f(\widehat{u},v). (55)

The fast-manifold identity (36) becomes

h⁡(0,v)=0for every admissible ​v.h(0,v)=0\quad\text{for every admissible }v. (56)

Thus a tangential displacement vv cannot create an order-one forcing in the normal equation while u^=0\widehat{u}=0. The only such forcing visible in (55) carries the explicit factor ρ\rho. A one-timescale norm bound for the stacked system obscures these factors.

There is an exact discrete counterpart. Abbreviate

Hk=H⁡(Yk,xk,θk),Fk=F⁡(Yk,xk,θk).H_{k}=H(Y_{k},x_{k},\theta_{k}),\qquad F_{k}=F(Y_{k},x_{k},\theta_{k}). (57)

Set Δk=θk+1−θk=η​ρ​Fk\Delta_{k}=\theta_{k+1}-\theta_{k}=\eta\rho F_{k}. Whenever the segment [θk,θk+1][\theta_{k},\theta_{k+1}] lies in the domain of the chosen C2C^{2} extension of λ\lambda, applying the fundamental theorem of calculus twice gives

λ⁡(θk+Δk)−λ⁡(θk)\displaystyle\lambda(\theta_{k}+\Delta_{k})-\lambda(\theta_{k}) =∫01Dθ​λ​(θk+s​Δk)​Δk​𝑑s\displaystyle=\int_{0}^{1}D_{\theta}\lambda(\theta_{k}+s\Delta_{k})\Delta_{k}\,ds
=Dθ​λ​(θk)​Δk+∫01∫0sDθ2​λ​(θk+t​Δk)​[Δk,Δk]​𝑑t​𝑑s\displaystyle=D_{\theta}\lambda(\theta_{k})\Delta_{k}+\int_{0}^{1}\int_{0}^{s}D_{\theta}^{2}\lambda(\theta_{k}+t\Delta_{k})[\Delta_{k},\Delta_{k}]\,dt\,ds
=Dθ​λ​(θk)​Δk+∫01(1−s)​Dθ2​λ​(θk+s​Δk)​[Δk,Δk]​ds.\displaystyle=D_{\theta}\lambda(\theta_{k})\Delta_{k}+\int_{0}^{1}(1-s)D_{\theta}^{2}\lambda(\theta_{k}+s\Delta_{k})[\Delta_{k},\Delta_{k}]\,ds.

The last equality interchanges the order of integration. Subtracting this identity from xk+1−xk=η​Hkx_{k+1}-x_{k}=\eta H_{k} gives

u^k+1−u^k=\displaystyle\widehat{u}_{k+1}-\widehat{u}_{k}={} η​Hk−η​ρ​Dθ​λ​(θk)​Fk\displaystyle\eta H_{k}-\eta\rho D_{\theta}\lambda(\theta_{k})F_{k}
−η2ρ2∫01(1−s)Dθ2λ(θk+sηρFk)[Fk,Fk]ds,\displaystyle-\eta^{2}\rho^{2}\int_{0}^{1}(1-s)D_{\theta}^{2}\lambda(\theta_{k}+s\eta\rho F_{k})[F_{k},F_{k}]\,ds, (58)
vk+1−vk=\displaystyle v_{k+1}-v_{k}={} η​ρ​Fk.\displaystyle\eta\rho F_{k}. (59)

Here Dθ2​λ​(θ)​[a,b]∈ℝdxD_{\theta}^{2}\lambda(\theta)[a,b]\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{x}} is a vector-valued bilinear second derivative. The factor 1/21/2 is already contained in ∫01(1−s)​𝑑s=1/2\int_{0}^{1}(1-s)\,ds=1/2. No derivative of FkF_{k} enters: FkF_{k} is held fixed as the direction of the one-step increment. This identity involves no asymptotic approximation.

Because u^k=xk−λ⁡(θk)\widehat{u}_{k}=x_{k}-\lambda(\theta_{k}), updating θk\theta_{k} also changes the reference fast equilibrium λ⁡(θk)\lambda(\theta_{k}). The first-order contribution of this change to the tracking error is −η​ρ​Dθ​λ​(θk)​Fk-\eta\rho D_{\theta}\lambda(\theta_{k})F_{k}, which has prefactor η​ρ\eta\rho. The curvature remainder in (58) accounts for the nonlinear part of this change and has prefactor η2​ρ2\eta^{2}\rho^{2}. After division by η\eta to express increments per unit of fast time, these prefactors become ρ\rho and η​ρ2\eta\rho^{2}, respectively. The curvature remainder therefore contains an additional step-size factor as well as two powers of ρ\rho. If the remaining coefficient factors are uniformly controlled, integration against a slow kernel gives the scaling estimates

∫0∞e−c​ρ​t​ρ​𝑑t=1c,∫0∞e−c​ρ​t​η​ρ2​𝑑t=η​ρc.\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-c\rho t}\rho\,dt=\frac{1}{c},\qquad\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-c\rho t}\eta\rho^{2}\,dt=\frac{\eta\rho}{c}.

The preceding integrals illustrate how a factor ρ\rho in a forcing term offsets the factor 1/ρ1/\rho arising from slow relaxation. The stationary covariance proof verifies this cancellation directly in the fixed tangent coordinates (u,v)(u,v). When the covariance equation is partitioned according to these coordinates, its (v,v)(v,v) block corresponds to covariances between components of the slow variable v=θ−θ⋆v=\theta-\theta^{\star}. We call this the slow–slow block.

The remainder in this block is O⁡(ρ​η3/2)O(\rho\eta^{3/2}), as shown in (104). The inverse estimate in Lemma 6 weights this remainder by 1/ρ1/\rho. The factor ρ\rho in the remainder therefore cancels this weight, giving an O⁡(η3/2)O(\eta^{3/2}) contribution to the covariance error, uniformly in sufficiently small positive ρ\rho.

B.2 Linearization at the Equilibrium

Recall the four Jacobian blocks at z⋆z^{\star} introduced in Subsection 2.1:

A=Dx​H¯​(z⋆),B=Dθ​H¯​(z⋆),C=Dx​F¯​(z⋆),D=Dθ​F¯​(z⋆).A=D_{x}\bar{H}(z^{\star}),\quad B=D_{\theta}\bar{H}(z^{\star}),\quad C=D_{x}\bar{F}(z^{\star}),\quad D=D_{\theta}\bar{F}(z^{\star}). (60)

Differentiating (36) at θ⋆\theta^{\star} gives

A​Λ+B=0,Λ=D​λ​(θ⋆)=−A−1​B.A\Lambda+B=0,\qquad\Lambda=D\lambda(\theta^{\star})=-A^{-1}B. (61)

The inverse A−1A^{-1} is available when the frozen fast equilibrium is locally exponentially stable. The reduced field was defined in equation 37 by g⁡(θ)=F¯​(λ⁡(θ),θ)g(\theta)=\bar{F}(\lambda(\theta),\theta). Its chain rule is

Dθ​g​(θ⋆)=Dx​F¯​(x⋆,θ⋆)​Dθ​λ​(θ⋆)+Dθ​F¯​(x⋆,θ⋆).D_{\theta}g(\theta^{\star})=D_{x}\bar{F}(x^{\star},\theta^{\star})D_{\theta}\lambda(\theta^{\star})+D_{\theta}\bar{F}(x^{\star},\theta^{\star}).

Substituting the Jacobian blocks gives

S=D​g​(θ⋆)=C​Λ+D=D−C​A−1​B.S=Dg(\theta^{\star})=C\Lambda+D=D-CA^{-1}B. (62)

For the local calculation, use the tangent coordinates (u,v)(u,v) of (44). Write δ​x=x−x⋆\delta x=x-x^{\star} and δ​θ=θ−θ⋆\delta\theta=\theta-\theta^{\star}. Retaining the first-order terms of the fast-clock ODE at z⋆z^{\star} gives the first-variation system

dd​t​(δ​xδ​θ)=(ABρ​Cρ​D)​(δ​xδ​θ),\frac{d}{dt}\begin{pmatrix}\delta x\\ \delta\theta\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\ \rho C&\rho D\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}\delta x\\ \delta\theta\end{pmatrix}, (63)

For finite deviations with r=‖(δ​x,δ​θ)‖r=\|(\delta x,\delta\theta)\|, the omitted remainders are O⁡(r2)O(r^{2}) in the first row and ρ​O​(r2)\rho O(r^{2}) in the second. Now substitute δ​x=u+Λ​v\delta x=u+\Lambda v. The lower row gives

v˙=ρ​C​(u+Λ​v)+ρ​D​v=ρ​C​u+ρ⁡(C​Λ+D)​v=ρ​C​u+ρ​S​v.\dot{v}=\rho C(u+\Lambda v)+\rho Dv=\rho Cu+\rho(C\Lambda+D)v=\rho Cu+\rho Sv.

Because Λ\Lambda is fixed in this tangent-coordinate calculation, u˙=δ​x˙−Λ​v˙\dot{u}=\dot{\delta x}-\Lambda\dot{v}. Thus

u˙\displaystyle\dot{u} =A⁡(u+Λ​v)+B​v−Λ⁡{ρ​C​(u+Λ​v)+ρ​D​v}\displaystyle=A(u+\Lambda v)+Bv-\Lambda\{\rho C(u+\Lambda v)+\rho Dv\}
=(A−ρ​Λ​C)​u+{A​Λ+B−ρ​Λ​(C​Λ+D)}​v\displaystyle=(A-\rho\Lambda C)u+\{A\Lambda+B-\rho\Lambda(C\Lambda+D)\}v
=(A−ρ​Λ​C)​u−ρ​Λ​S​v.\displaystyle=(A-\rho\Lambda C)u-\rho\Lambda Sv.

The identities A​Λ+B=0A\Lambda+B=0 and C​Λ+D=SC\Lambda+D=S therefore give

dd​t​(uv)=Lρ​(uv),Lρ=(A−ρ​Λ​C−ρ​Λ​Sρ​Cρ​S).\frac{d}{dt}\begin{pmatrix}u\\ v\end{pmatrix}=L_{\rho}\begin{pmatrix}u\\ v\end{pmatrix},\qquad L_{\rho}=\begin{pmatrix}A-\rho\Lambda C&-\rho\Lambda S\\ \rho C&\rho S\end{pmatrix}. (64)

Every off-diagonal interaction in these coordinates has a factor ρ\rho. At ρ=0\rho=0, the uu-block is the stable matrix AA and the vv-block is frozen. For small positive ρ\rho, the diagonal slow block ρ​S\rho S is Hurwitz, and the complete slow equation is v˙=ρ​S​v+ρ​C​u\dot{v}=\rho Sv+\rho Cu. The term ρ​C​u\rho Cu describes the coupling from the fast deviation to the slow variable.

B.3 Two-Clock Semigroup Bounds

We now quantify relaxation in the linearized system: et​Lρe^{tL_{\rho}} maps the initial deviation (u⁡(0),v⁡(0))(u(0),v(0)) to (u⁡(t),v⁡(t))(u(t),v(t)). The proof separates fast and slow invariant subspaces to obtain bounds that retain both relaxation rates and the factors ρ\rho in their interactions, uniformly for small positive ρ\rho, for both the ODE and its Euler discretization.

Proposition 1 (Two-clock semigroup bounds; restatement).

Under and , there exist constants C∗,c,ρ0>0C_{*},c,\rho_{0}>0, independent of ρ\rho, such that for 0<ρ≤ρ00<\rho\leq\rho_{0} and t≥0t\geq 0,

‖[et​Lρ]u​u‖\displaystyle\|[e^{tL_{\rho}}]_{uu}\| ≤C∗​(e−c​t+ρ​e−c​ρ​t),\displaystyle\leq C_{*}\bigl(e^{-ct}+\rho e^{-c\rho t}\bigr), (65)
‖[et​Lρ]u​v‖+‖[et​Lρ]v​u‖\displaystyle\|[e^{tL_{\rho}}]_{uv}\|+\|[e^{tL_{\rho}}]_{vu}\| ≤C∗​ρ​(e−c​t+e−c​ρ​t),\displaystyle\leq C_{*}\rho\bigl(e^{-ct}+e^{-c\rho t}\bigr),
‖[et​Lρ]v​v‖\displaystyle\|[e^{tL_{\rho}}]_{vv}\| ≤C∗​e−c​ρ​t.\displaystyle\leq C_{*}e^{-c\rho t}.

The same bounds hold for (I+η​Lρ)k(I+\eta L_{\rho})^{k}, with t=η​kt=\eta k, uniformly for sufficiently small η\eta and integers k≥0k\geq 0.

The block subscripts specify the output and input coordinates, in that order. Thus [et​Lρ]u​v[e^{tL_{\rho}}]_{uv} gives the contribution to u⁡(t)u(t) from the initial slow deviation v⁡(0)v(0), while [et​Lρ]v​u[e^{tL_{\rho}}]_{vu} gives the contribution to v⁡(t)v(t) from the initial fast deviation u⁡(0)u(0). The factors e−c​te^{-ct} and e−c​ρ​te^{-c\rho t} describe fast and slow relaxation, respectively.

Proof.

Write the blocks of LρL_{\rho} as

Lρ=(AρℬρCρDρ′),Aρ=A−ρ​Λ​C,ℬρ=−ρ​Λ​S,Cρ=ρ​C,Dρ′=ρ​S.L_{\rho}=\begin{pmatrix}A_{\rho}&\mathcal{B}_{\rho}\\ C_{\rho}&D_{\rho}^{\prime}\end{pmatrix},\quad A_{\rho}=A-\rho\Lambda C,\quad\mathcal{B}_{\rho}=-\rho\Lambda S,\quad C_{\rho}=\rho C,\quad D_{\rho}^{\prime}=\rho S.

We seek invariant subspaces of the form u=Xρ​vu=X_{\rho}v and v=Rρ​uv=R_{\rho}u: a solution starting in either subspace remains there. These describe the perturbed slow and fast subspaces, respectively. Their invariance equations are

Aρ​Xρ+ℬρ−Xρ​(Cρ​Xρ+Dρ′)\displaystyle A_{\rho}X_{\rho}+\mathcal{B}_{\rho}-X_{\rho}(C_{\rho}X_{\rho}+D_{\rho}^{\prime}) =0,\displaystyle=0,
Cρ+Dρ′​Rρ−Rρ​(Aρ+ℬρ​Rρ)\displaystyle C_{\rho}+D_{\rho}^{\prime}R_{\rho}-R_{\rho}(A_{\rho}+\mathcal{B}_{\rho}R_{\rho}) =0.\displaystyle=0.

At ρ=0\rho=0, the derivatives in XX and RR are respectively X↦A​XX\mapsto AX and R↦−R​AR\mapsto-RA, both invertible. The implicit-function theorem therefore gives Xρ,Rρ=O⁡(ρ)X_{\rho},R_{\rho}=O(\rho). The matrix

Qρ=(IXρRρI)Q_{\rho}=\begin{pmatrix}I&X_{\rho}\\ R_{\rho}&I\end{pmatrix}

is uniformly invertible for small ρ\rho, and

Qρ−1​Lρ​Qρ=diag⁡(Af​(ρ),ρ​Ss​(ρ)),Af=Aρ+ℬρ​Rρ=A+O⁡(ρ),Ss=S+C​Xρ=S+O⁡(ρ).Q_{\rho}^{-1}L_{\rho}Q_{\rho}=\operatorname{diag}(A_{f}(\rho),\rho S_{s}(\rho)),\quad A_{f}=A_{\rho}+\mathcal{B}_{\rho}R_{\rho}=A+O(\rho),\quad S_{s}=S+CX_{\rho}=S+O(\rho).

Fixed quadratic Lyapunov functions for the Hurwitz matrices AA and SS remain strict Lyapunov functions for these perturbations. Consequently,

‖et​Af‖≤C​e−c​t,‖eρ​t​Ss‖≤C​e−c​ρ​t,\|e^{tA_{f}}\|\leq Ce^{-ct},\qquad\|e^{\rho tS_{s}}\|\leq Ce^{-c\rho t},

with constants independent of ρ\rho. Finally, writing Qρ=I+EρQ_{\rho}=I+E_{\rho}, where EρE_{\rho} has only off-diagonal blocks of size O⁡(ρ)O(\rho), the Neumann series Qρ−1=I−Eρ+Eρ2−⋯Q_{\rho}^{-1}=I-E_{\rho}+E_{\rho}^{2}-\cdots shows that its diagonal corrections are O⁡(ρ2)O(\rho^{2}) and its off-diagonal blocks are O⁡(ρ)O(\rho). Multiplication in et​Lρ=Qρ​diag⁡(et​Af,eρ​t​Ss)​Qρ−1e^{tL_{\rho}}=Q_{\rho}\operatorname{diag}(e^{tA_{f}},e^{\rho tS_{s}})Q_{\rho}^{-1} then preserves the two clocks and the small cross factors. Multiplying the block matrices proves (65); in fact, the upper-left slow contribution and lower-right fast contribution are both O⁡(ρ2)O(\rho^{2}).

For completeness, the same Lyapunov functions give, uniformly for small η\eta, contraction factors 1−c​η1-c\eta and 1−c​η​ρ1-c\eta\rho for the squared Lyapunov norms of I+η​AfI+\eta A_{f} and I+η​ρ​SsI+\eta\rho S_{s}, respectively. Indeed, if PfP_{f} is the fixed fast Lyapunov matrix, then

(I+η​Af)⊤​Pf​(I+η​Af)−Pf=η⁡(Af⊤​Pf+Pf​Af)+η2​Af⊤​Pf​Af⪯−c​η​Pf,(I+\eta A_{f})^{\top}P_{f}(I+\eta A_{f})-P_{f}=\eta(A_{f}^{\top}P_{f}+P_{f}A_{f})+\eta^{2}A_{f}^{\top}P_{f}A_{f}\preceq-c\eta P_{f},

after decreasing η0\eta_{0}; the slow argument is identical with η\eta replaced by η​ρ\eta\rho. Thus the same block bounds hold for (I+η​Lρ)k(I+\eta L_{\rho})^{k}, with t=η​kt=\eta k. ∎

The upper equation of equation 64 is

u˙=(A−ρ​Λ​C)​u−ρ​Λ​S​v.\dot{u}=(A-\rho\Lambda C)u-\rho\Lambda Sv.

To isolate the upper-right channel, consider a one-way scalar model with coupling β\beta and stable rates −a,−s-a,-s. Prescribe the uncoupled slow response v⁡(t)=e−ρ​s​t​v0v(t)=e^{-\rho st}v_{0} and solve

u˙=−a​u+ρ​β​v,a,s>0.\dot{u}=-au+\rho\beta v,\qquad a,s>0. (66)

Then

u⁡(t)\displaystyle u(t) =e−a​t​u0+ρ​β​v0​∫0te−a⁡(t−r)​e−ρ​s​r​𝑑r\displaystyle=e^{-at}u_{0}+\rho\beta v_{0}\int_{0}^{t}e^{-a(t-r)}e^{-\rho sr}\,dr
=e−a​t​u0+ρ​β​v0​e−ρ​s​t−e−a​ta−ρ​s.\displaystyle=e^{-at}u_{0}+\rho\beta v_{0}\frac{e^{-\rho st}-e^{-at}}{a-\rho s}. (67)

For small ρ\rho, the denominator is bounded away from zero and the slow tail in uu has amplitude O⁡(ρ)O(\rho). The reverse channel is illustrated by a scalar coupling γ\gamma in v˙=−ρ​s​v+ρ​γ​u\dot{v}=-\rho sv+\rho\gamma u. Prescribing the uncoupled fast response u⁡(t)=e−a​t​u0u(t)=e^{-at}u_{0} gives

v˙+ρ​s​v=ρ​γ​u0​e−a​t,dd​t​{eρ​s​t​v​(t)}=ρ​γ​u0​e(ρ​s−a)​t.\dot{v}+\rho sv=\rho\gamma u_{0}e^{-at},\qquad\frac{d}{dt}\{e^{\rho st}v(t)\}=\rho\gamma u_{0}e^{(\rho s-a)t}.

Integrating from zero to tt, for a≠ρ​sa\neq\rho s,

eρ​s​t​v​(t)−v0=ρ​γ​u0​e(ρ​s−a)​t−1ρ​s−a.e^{\rho st}v(t)-v_{0}=\rho\gamma u_{0}\frac{e^{(\rho s-a)t}-1}{\rho s-a}.

Multiplication by e−ρ​s​te^{-\rho st} yields

v⁡(t)=e−ρ​s​t​v0+ρ​γ​u0​e−ρ​s​t−e−a​ta−ρ​s,v(t)=e^{-\rho st}v_{0}+\rho\gamma u_{0}\frac{e^{-\rho st}-e^{-at}}{a-\rho s}, (68)

which again has cross amplitude O⁡(ρ)O(\rho) for sufficiently small ρ\rho. At the exceptional resonant value a=ρ​sa=\rho s, the continuous limiting formula is

v⁡(t)=e−a​t​{v0+ρ​γ​u0​t}.v(t)=e^{-at}\{v_{0}+\rho\gamma u_{0}t\}.

The same denominator caveat applies to equation 67; at resonance its convolution is t​e−a​tte^{-at}. One may choose ρ0<a/s\rho_{0}<a/s to avoid resonance throughout the small-ratio range. These one-way formulas illustrate the two cross bounds in equation 65.

The slow exponential integrates to O⁡(1/ρ)O(1/\rho) on the fast clock:

∫0∞e−c​ρ​t​𝑑t=1c​ρ.\int_{0}^{\infty}e^{-c\rho t}\,dt=\frac{1}{c\rho}. (69)

If a forcing term has size O⁡(ρ)O(\rho) with a constant independent of ρ\rho, integration against this slow exponential gives an O⁡(1)O(1) bound. Discarding the factor ρ\rho before integration can therefore introduce an unnecessary factor 1/ρ1/\rho in the estimate.

Returning to iteration number kk, t=k​ηt=k\eta changes the two exponentials into

e−c​η​kande−c​ρ​η​k=e−c​ε​k.e^{-c\eta k}\quad\text{and}\quad e^{-c\rho\eta k}=e^{-c\varepsilon k}. (70)

These linear bounds identify the fast and slow relaxation rates relevant to initialization effects. Quantitative initialization bounds for the nonlinear stochastic recursion are developed in Appendix I under the two-clock coupling conditions. Stationary bias calculations start from an invariant law and do not require an initialization estimate.

Appendix C Poisson tools and Taylor estimates

We first compute the long-run covariance QQ of the noise ξk=G⁡(Yk,z⋆)\xi_{k}=G(Y_{k},z^{\star}), obtained by holding the algorithmic state at the equilibrium z⋆z^{\star} while the Markov chain continues to evolve (Subsection C.1). Because successive Markov inputs are correlated, the accumulated noise fluctuations depend on correlations across time, which QQ records. This matrix supplies the noise term in the Lyapunov equation for the leading stationary covariance of the iterates. That covariance enters the quadratic Taylor terms of the averaged drift and therefore determines the curvature contribution to the stationary mean bias.

Next, for a fixed algorithmic state zz, we use the Poisson equation to decompose the centered Markov update into a martingale difference and a telescoping correction, whose sum reduces to initial and final terms (Subsection C.2). We then derive Taylor estimates for the nonlinear remainder terms and for changes in the Poisson solution as the algorithmic state evolves (Subsection C.3). Appendix D uses these tools to establish the stationary covariance and mean-bias expansions.

C.1 Long-Run Covariance of the Markov Noise

Recall the compact recursion

zk+1=zk+η​Dρ​G​(Yk,zk),z_{k+1}=z_{k}+\eta D_{\rho}G(Y_{k},z_{k}),

where z=(x,θ)z=(x,\theta), Dρ=diag⁡(I,ρ​I)D_{\rho}=\operatorname{diag}(I,\rho I), and ρ=ε/η\rho=\varepsilon/\eta. Average the update over the stationary law μ\mu of the exogenous Markov chain:

G¯​(z)=∑yμ⁡(y)​G​(y,z), define G~​(y,z)=G⁡(y,z)−G¯​(z).\bar{G}(z)=\sum_{y}\mu(y)G(y,z),\qquad\mbox{ define }\qquad\widetilde{G}(y,z)=G(y,z)-\bar{G}(z). (71)

At the averaged equilibrium z⋆z^{\star}, we have G¯​(z⋆)=0\bar{G}(z^{\star})=0. The update noise frozen at that point is therefore

ξk=G⁡(Yk,z⋆)=G~​(Yk,z⋆).\xi_{k}=G(Y_{k},z^{\star})=\widetilde{G}(Y_{k},z^{\star}). (72)

For each fixed zz, G~​(⋅,z)\widetilde{G}(\cdot,z) is centered under μ\mu.

In Sections C.1 and C.2, expectations refer to the stationary Markov path: Y0∼μY_{0}\sim\mu, followed by transitions with kernel PP. In particular, 𝔼​ξk=0\mathbb{E}\xi_{k}=0. This convention specifies the noise covariance without requiring stationary initialization of the algorithm.

With Markov data the variance of a long sum contains all cross-time covariances, so the relevant matrix is

Q=limm→∞1m​𝔼​[(∑k=0m−1ξk)​(∑k=0m−1ξk)⊤].Q=\lim_{m\to\infty}\frac{1}{m}\mathbb{E}\left[\left(\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\xi_{k}\right)\left(\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\xi_{k}\right)^{\!\top}\right]. (73)

Thus QQ is the covariance accumulated per step. Write Sm=∑k=0m−1ξkS_{m}=\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\xi_{k} and Kh=𝔼⁡[ξ0​ξh⊤]K_{h}=\mathbb{E}[\xi_{0}\xi_{h}^{\top}]. Since the sum is centered,

Cov⁡(Sm)=𝔼⁡[Sm​Sm⊤]=∑i=0m−1∑j=0m−1𝔼⁡[ξi​ξj⊤].\operatorname{Cov}(S_{m})=\mathbb{E}[S_{m}S_{m}^{\top}]=\sum_{i=0}^{m-1}\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}\mathbb{E}[\xi_{i}\xi_{j}^{\top}].

Stationarity makes each diagonal term equal to K0K_{0}. For a positive lag hh, the m−hm-h pairs with j=i+hj=i+h each contribute KhK_{h}, whereas the m−hm-h reversed pairs each contribute Kh⊤K_{h}^{\top}. Thus the exact finite-sum identity is

1m​𝔼​[Sm​Sm⊤]=K0+∑h=1m−1(1−hm)​(Kh+Kh⊤).\frac{1}{m}\mathbb{E}[S_{m}S_{m}^{\top}]=K_{0}+\sum_{h=1}^{m-1}\left(1-\frac{h}{m}\right)(K_{h}+K_{h}^{\top}).

Suppose ∑h≥1‖Kh‖<∞\sum_{h\geq 1}\|K_{h}\|<\infty. For every fixed hh, the factor 𝟏{h<m}(1−h/m)\mathbf{1}_{\{h<m\}}(1-h/m) tends to one and lies in [0,1][0,1]. The norm of the corresponding summand is bounded by 2​‖Kh‖2\|K_{h}\|, a summable sequence. The dominated convergence theorem for series, applied entrywise with summable dominating sequence 2​‖Kh‖2\|K_{h}\|, therefore gives

Q=K0+∑h=1∞(Kh+Kh⊤).Q=K_{0}+\sum_{h=1}^{\infty}\bigl(K_{h}+K_{h}^{\top}\bigr). (74)

The summability condition follows from Assumption . Indeed, on the finite state space the centered function ξ⁡(y)=G⁡(y,z⋆)\xi(y)=G(y,z^{\star}) is bounded. Geometric mixing gives constants C<∞C<\infty and r∈(0,1)r\in(0,1) such that

supy‖(Ph​ξ)​(y)‖≤C​rh​maxy​‖ξ⁡(y)‖.\sup_{y}\|(P^{h}\xi)(y)\|\leq Cr^{h}\max_{y}\|\xi(y)\|.

Conditioning on Y0Y_{0} then gives

Kh=∑yμ⁡(y)​ξ​(y)​(Ph​ξ)​(y)⊤,‖Kh‖≤C​rh​(maxy⁡‖ξ⁡(y)‖)2.K_{h}=\sum_{y}\mu(y)\xi(y)(P^{h}\xi)(y)^{\top},\qquad\|K_{h}\|\leq Cr^{h}\bigl(\max_{y}\|\xi(y)\|\bigr)^{2}.

Consequently, (74) holds here. Stationarity alone would not suffice: for the stationary alternating chain Yk+1=−YkY_{k+1}=-Y_{k}, with equally likely initial signs and ξk=Yk\xi_{k}=Y_{k}, the partial sums are bounded and Q=0Q=0, but Kh=(−1)hK_{h}=(-1)^{h} makes the displayed infinite series divergent. That periodic chain is excluded by geometric mixing.

By contrast, 𝔼⁡[m−1​∑k<mξk​ξk⊤]=K0\mathbb{E}[m^{-1}\sum_{k<m}\xi_{k}\xi_{k}^{\top}]=K_{0} omits every off-diagonal term, so QQ generally differs from the one-step covariance.

C.2 Martingale Decomposition via the Poisson Equation

For a function aa of the Markov state, define

(P​a)​(y)=∑y′P⁡(y,y′)​a​(y′).(Pa)(y)=\sum_{y^{\prime}}P(y,y^{\prime})a(y^{\prime}).

This is the conditional mean of a⁡(Yk+1)a(Y_{k+1}) given Yk=yY_{k}=y.

For each fixed value of zz consider the following equation

𝒰⁡(y,z)−(P​𝒰)​(y,z)=G~​(y,z),∑yμ⁡(y)​𝒰​(y,z)=0.\mathcal{U}(y,z)-(P\mathcal{U})(y,z)=\widetilde{G}(y,z),\qquad\sum_{y}\mu(y)\mathcal{U}(y,z)=0. (75)

This is the Poisson equation. The second condition chooses one solution by forcing its stationary mean to be zero. For a finite-state geometrically ergodic chain, the solution is

𝒰⁡(⋅,z)=∑j=0∞Pj​G~​(⋅,z).\mathcal{U}(\,\cdot\,,z)=\sum_{j=0}^{\infty}P^{j}\widetilde{G}(\,\cdot\,,z). (76)

Define the one-step innovation

ζk+1​(z)=𝒰⁡(Yk+1,z)−(P​𝒰)​(Yk,z).\zeta_{k+1}(z)=\mathcal{U}(Y_{k+1},z)-(P\mathcal{U})(Y_{k},z). (77)

Let ℱk\mathcal{F}_{k} contain the iterate and the complete Markov history up to time kk. Exogeneity means that, given YkY_{k}, the next Markov state does not depend on the rest of ℱk\mathcal{F}_{k}. Therefore

𝔼⁡[ζk+1​(z)∣ℱk]=0.\mathbb{E}[\zeta_{k+1}(z)\mid\mathcal{F}_{k}]=0. (78)

Indeed, conditional on YkY_{k}, the expected value of 𝒰⁡(Yk+1,z)\mathcal{U}(Y_{k+1},z) is exactly (P​𝒰)​(Yk,z)(P\mathcal{U})(Y_{k},z).

The Poisson equation can now be rearranged as

G~​(Yk,z)=𝒰⁡(Yk,z)−𝒰⁡(Yk+1,z)+ζk+1​(z).\widetilde{G}(Y_{k},z)=\mathcal{U}(Y_{k},z)-\mathcal{U}(Y_{k+1},z)+\zeta_{k+1}(z). (79)

Summing this identity makes the first two terms cancel across time:

∑k=0m−1G~​(Yk,z)=𝒰⁡(Y0,z)−𝒰⁡(Ym,z)+∑k=0m−1ζk+1​(z).\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\widetilde{G}(Y_{k},z)=\mathcal{U}(Y_{0},z)-\mathcal{U}(Y_{m},z)+\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\zeta_{k+1}(z). (80)

The endpoint difference remains bounded in mean square. The martingale sum has root-mean-square size O⁡(m)O(\sqrt{m}). Fix z=z⋆z=z^{\star} and write

Mm=∑k=0m−1ζk+1(z⋆),Bm=𝒰(Y0,z⋆)−𝒰(Ym,z⋆),Qζ=𝔼⁡[ζ1​(z⋆)​ζ1​(z⋆)⊤].\begin{gathered}M_{m}=\sum_{k=0}^{m-1}\zeta_{k+1}(z^{\star}),\qquad B_{m}=\mathcal{U}(Y_{0},z^{\star})-\mathcal{U}(Y_{m},z^{\star}),\\ Q_{\zeta}=\mathbb{E}[\zeta_{1}(z^{\star})\zeta_{1}(z^{\star})^{\top}].\end{gathered}

Thus Sm=Mm+BmS_{m}=M_{m}+B_{m}. For i<ji<j, the vector ζi​(z⋆)\zeta_{i}(z^{\star}) is measurable with respect to ℱj−1\mathcal{F}_{j-1}, so

𝔼⁡[ζi​(z⋆)​ζj​(z⋆)⊤]=𝔼⁡[ζi​(z⋆)​𝔼​[ζj​(z⋆)⊤∣ℱj−1]]=0.\mathbb{E}[\zeta_{i}(z^{\star})\zeta_{j}(z^{\star})^{\top}]=\mathbb{E}\!\left[\zeta_{i}(z^{\star})\mathbb{E}[\zeta_{j}(z^{\star})^{\top}\mid\mathcal{F}_{j-1}]\right]=0.

The expectation with the indices reversed is also zero:

𝔼⁡[ζj​(z⋆)​ζi​(z⋆)⊤]=(𝔼⁡[ζi​(z⋆)​ζj​(z⋆)⊤])⊤=0.\mathbb{E}[\zeta_{j}(z^{\star})\zeta_{i}(z^{\star})^{\top}]=\left(\mathbb{E}[\zeta_{i}(z^{\star})\zeta_{j}(z^{\star})^{\top}]\right)^{\top}=0.

Since the Markov input chain is stationary (Y0∼μY_{0}\sim\mu), the pair (Yk,Yk+1)(Y_{k},Y_{k+1}) has the same distribution for every kk. At the fixed state z⋆z^{\star}, each innovation is the same function of this pair. Consequently,

𝔼⁡[ζk+1​(z⋆)​ζk+1​(z⋆)⊤]=Qζfor every ​k≥0.\mathbb{E}[\zeta_{k+1}(z^{\star})\zeta_{k+1}(z^{\star})^{\top}]=Q_{\zeta}\qquad\text{for every }k\geq 0.

Expanding the square therefore yields

𝔼[MmMm⊤]=mQζ,𝔼∥Mm∥2=mtrQζ,‖Mm‖L2=m​tr⁡Qζ,\begin{gathered}\mathbb{E}[M_{m}M_{m}^{\top}]=mQ_{\zeta},\qquad\mathbb{E}\|M_{m}\|^{2}=m\operatorname{tr}Q_{\zeta},\\ \|M_{m}\|_{L^{2}}=\sqrt{m\operatorname{tr}Q_{\zeta}},\end{gathered}

where ‖X‖L2=(𝔼​‖X‖2)1/2\|X\|_{L^{2}}=(\mathbb{E}\|X\|^{2})^{1/2}. This proves the O⁡(m)O(\sqrt{m}) assertion in L2L^{2}. Since 𝔼​(a⊤​Mm)2=m​a⊤​Qζ​a\mathbb{E}(a^{\top}M_{m})^{2}=m\,a^{\top}Q_{\zeta}a, the scale is nondegenerate in a direction aa if and only if a⊤​Qζ​a>0a^{\top}Q_{\zeta}a>0.

The correction BmB_{m} consists of the values of the Poisson solution at the initial and final Markov states, Y0Y_{0} and YmY_{m}. 1m​𝔼​[Sm​Sm⊤]−Qζ=1m​𝔼​[Mm​Bm⊤+Bm​Mm⊤+Bm​Bm⊤].\frac{1}{m}\mathbb{E}[S_{m}S_{m}^{\top}]-Q_{\zeta}=\frac{1}{m}\mathbb{E}[M_{m}B_{m}^{\top}+B_{m}M_{m}^{\top}+B_{m}B_{m}^{\top}].

Lemma 3 (Poisson representation).

Under , the innovations (77) are martingale differences, and the long-run covariance (73) satisfies

Let Yk∈{−1,1}Y_{k}\in\{-1,1\} be a stationary symmetric two-state Markov chain, with

Fix ω∈ℝd\omega\in\mathbb{R}^{d}, d=dx+dθd=d_{x}+d_{\theta}, and take G~​(y,z⋆)=ω​y\widetilde{G}(y,z^{\star})=\omega y. The frozen noise is ξk=ω​Yk\xi_{k}=\omega Y_{k}, and the Poisson solution is
